notes: The one voice of Ashwell (hearthvale), written with the atlas: The notch on the well-house post is above last year's for the first time in a century, and the well-warden wants someone to walk the glass bed to the Choir and say why.

greetings.text: The notch did not move this spring. I have not decided yet whether to thank you. Sit, drink; the water is clean, and I would like somebody to be glad of it.
She came up again on Hushday. I filled the flask for her and put it on the lip and went inside. The notch is a finger higher. I cut it true.

Two knights came up the bed with a bell and walked her back down. They did not say where to. The Order does not say, and I have stopped asking, because they looked sorry, and a sorry knight is a rare thing.
They said somebody came up the Stair. I did not believe it. I have been wrong about the grey this year, so I am trying to believe things.

greet.speaker: Ada Welling
greet.text: Welling. Ada. You have come up out of the grey road, haven't you; it is on your boots. Sit, or drink, or both. The water is the first clean water north of the ash and it tastes of the chalk, and that is the point of it.

hub.speaker: Ada Welling
hub.text: What is it you want to know? Everybody here wants to know something.

choices.text: What are the notches on the door-post?
What is south of here, for someone like you?
Is Ashwell on the Roll?
You wanted somebody to walk the bed to the Choir.
It is a pilgrim, Ada. Walking water back up the bed.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Ada Welling
topic_1.text: One a year, every Naming Day, since before my grandmother. I walk down the glass bed with the cord until the grass stops being green, and I cut the notch at that many knots. For a hundred years the notches went down the post, a little, and we said the Vale was winning. This year's is above last year's. I measured three times. — I have told the Wardens. They wrote it down. I would like somebody to walk the bed to the Choir and tell me what is coming up it.

topic_2.speaker: Ada Welling
topic_2.text: Down. We say down, in Ashwell, because the road goes down to the pool and the pool is where the water comes out of the glass. We do not say the other word. — The pilgrims say it. I fill their flasks at the Wellspring and they carry them down to pour out at the line, and I have filled nine hundred and forty flasks, and not one has come back up the road, and I would know.

topic_3.speaker: Ada Welling
topic_3.text: Eleven hearths, on the Wardens' Roll, read out every Tollday at the Rest. My brother is a Warden; he reads it some weeks, and he reads Ashwell a little louder than the rest, which I am told is not allowed and which I have told him I would notice if he stopped.

bye.speaker: Ada Welling
bye.text: Mind the bed on your way down, if it is down you are going. The glass cuts, and it cuts clean, and you do not feel it until you are home.

q_the_notch_on_the_post_offer.speaker: Ada Welling
q_the_notch_on_the_post_offer.text: I did, and I do. — The notch is above last year's. I measured three times. And this week a flask came back up: full, on the lip of the Wellspring, with my own tally cut in the neck. Nine hundred and twelve. I have filled nine hundred and forty and not one has come back up the road, and I would know. — Walk down the bed to the spring and bring it me, and then go on to the Greyline Stones and see where the grey begins. Ash Watch lit its beacon last night and nobody on its roll will own to it. Somebody is lying, or somebody is frightened, and in my experience it is the same somebody.

choices.text: I'll walk the bed.
Not now.

q_the_notch_on_the_post_accept.speaker: Ada Welling
q_the_notch_on_the_post_accept.text: Mind the glass. It cuts clean, and you do not feel it until you are home. — And if the Watch gives you their log, read all of it. The Wardens write down everything and then do not read it, and I have always thought that was a waste of good ink.

q_the_notch_on_the_post_decide_put_her_d.speaker: Ada Welling
q_the_notch_on_the_post_decide_put_her_d.text: Before dawn, then, at the lip. — Be quick with her. She was never quick with anything, and she would not want to be waited for.

q_the_notch_on_the_post_decide_let_her_w.speaker: Ada Welling
q_the_notch_on_the_post_decide_let_her_w.text: To somebody. — Yes. That is what a flask is for. I will cut the notch where the grey is and I will not pretend it is lower, and if it comes to the door I will fill her flask myself.

q_the_notch_on_the_post_decide_tell_the_.speaker: Ada Welling
q_the_notch_on_the_post_decide_tell_the_.text: Theirs. They read her name at Greywatch and she did not stay read. — Go to Pilgrim's Ash and tell the knight who keeps the night. They will want to know their Roll has a hole in it.

q_the_notch_on_the_post_decide.speaker: Ada Welling
q_the_notch_on_the_post_decide.text: ...Hild Marrow. Nine hundred and twelve. She had a laugh like a gate, and she bought bread off me for the road and gave half of it to the horses. — The grey comes up behind her. Every stride. — What would you have me do? You have seen it and I have only heard. I am asking you as the well-warden, and I will cut the notch at whatever you say.

choices.text: Put her down at the spring, before she fills another.
Let her walk. She is carrying water to somebody.
Tell the Order. She is theirs.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Ada Welling
work_going.text: The spring keeps me. The Vale has other work that wants hands. This is this week's.

notes: The one voice of Wynstead (hearthvale), written with the atlas: Someone has been opening the sluices at night, and the flood is drowning the lane where Gosford's name used to be; the sluice-keeper thinks that is the point.

greet.speaker: Hal Wynstead
greet.text: Wynstead. Hal. You are standing on the dry bit, which is the right bit to stand on in March. The meadows are under a hand of water and they will be under it till the grass is up, and the grass is why the Vale has hay.

hub.speaker: Hal Wynstead
hub.text: Ask, then. I am between sluices.

choices.text: Why flood a meadow on purpose?
You said someone opens the sluices at night.
What was Gosford like?
The twelfth sluice. I could sit the night with you.
The twelfth paddle was Gosford's.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Hal Wynstead
topic_1.text: The water is warmer than the air in March, so the grass under it wakes a month early; the Vale's hay comes off drowned ground and nobody in Merrowby who eats the mutton thinks about that once. My cousin Ellard used to. Then he learned to read ledgers and forgot how to read water, and now he sends me letters about the hay price.

topic_2.speaker: Hal Wynstead
topic_2.text: Three nights this month. Not the whole chain, just the twelfth, the one with no name, and the water runs west across the low meadow onto the old lane, the one that went to Gosford. — You have heard of Gosford. Nine hearths, gone in eleven days while the Toll hummed. The Toll is humming. Somebody is drowning the lane to it, and I have sat up two nights and seen nobody, and the paddle was open in the morning both times.

topic_3.speaker: Hal Wynstead
topic_3.text: I never saw it. Old Pellam did, at twenty-two, and found the doors on and the kettles on the hooks and nobody. The lane is still there, and it goes to a green, and the green goes to nothing, and I will not walk it, and I have walked every other yard of this Vale with water in my boots.

bye.speaker: Hal Wynstead
bye.text: If you are going west, keep off the low meadow. It looks like grass. It is a hand of water with grass in it.

q_the_twelfth_sluice_offer.speaker: Hal Wynstead
q_the_twelfth_sluice_offer.text: Would you. — I have sat two, and my knees are forty years older than the meadows and they told me so. It is the twelfth paddle, the one with no name on its post; my grandfather could not tell me why it had none and his grandfather would not. The water goes down the Gosford lane. Somebody wants that lane under water, and I would like to know who before the hay does.

choices.text: I'll sit the third night.
Not now.

q_the_twelfth_sluice_accept.speaker: Hal Wynstead
q_the_twelfth_sluice_accept.text: After dark, then, by the twelfth. Bring a coat; the water is warmer than the air, and it knows it. — If it is a Merrowby boy with a grudge, bring him to me. If it is not, do not bring it to me.

q_the_twelfth_sluice_decide_name_it.speaker: Hal Wynstead
q_the_twelfth_sluice_decide_name_it.text: Then I will cut it, and I will cut it deep, and my cousin can write to me about the hay price. A meadow that is watered is a meadow that is kept.

q_the_twelfth_sluice_decide_nail_it.speaker: Hal Wynstead
q_the_twelfth_sluice_decide_nail_it.text: Nailed, then. — It is the sensible thing, and I have been sensible for forty years, and I will pay you for your night because it was a night. I will not sleep better. I did not expect to.

q_the_twelfth_sluice_decide_tell_the_war.speaker: Hal Wynstead
q_the_twelfth_sluice_decide_tell_the_war.text: The Rest, then. They cut the name on their stone; they can keep an eye on what it opens. I will send the boy up in the morning. I will not go myself. I have walked every yard of this Vale with water in my boots except that one.

q_the_twelfth_sluice_decide.speaker: Hal Wynstead
q_the_twelfth_sluice_decide.text: Gosford's. — Well. Nine hearths, and they dug the twelfth cut with the rest of us, and we took their name off it the spring they went, as if a post could catch it. And now they come up the lane in the dark to water a meadow they cannot eat off. — I am a sluice-keeper. Tell me what the paddle is.

choices.text: Cut the name back. Let them water it on humming nights.
Nail it down. The hay is yours.
Give it to the Wardens. Let them watch the lane.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Hal Wynstead
work_going.text: Water does its own work. The rest of the Vale does not, and it pays for help. Here.

greetings.text: Twelve names on twelve posts. The Toll hummed on Hushday and the paddle lifted itself and I sat and watched it, with a coat on, and it was a good night.
The hay is the best in six years. You would think that would be the end of it.

The Rest sends a Warden down the lane on humming nights. She sits on the twelfth post with a book on her knee and writes down what she does not see. The paddle has not moved. I have stopped telling myself that is good news.

notes: The one voice of Cressbourne (hearthvale), written with the atlas: The top bed came up grey overnight, and the Cresswells want to know whether it is the water, the chalk or the Toll before the city tastes it.

greet.speaker: Lin Cresswell
greet.text: You are standing in my light. — Cresswell, Lin. The top bed is mine and the rest are my cousins' and every one of them is wrong about something.

hub.speaker: Lin Cresswell
hub.text: Well?

choices.text: What happened to the top bed?
Is it true Tollmere stole your sauce?
I'll find out what turned the top bed.
It is the water. Somebody was robbing the bridge.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Lin Cresswell
topic_1.text: It came up grey. Not dead: grey, as if somebody had drawn the green out of it with a thread. I tasted it. It tastes of nothing, which a cress should never do, it should taste of the chalk and the water and a little of cold iron. — The spring comes up under the top bed first. If it is the water, the other beds go next, one a week, down the coombe. If it is the chalk it will stop at the wall. If it is the Toll, I have no idea, and nor does anybody, and I would like somebody who does.

topic_2.speaker: Lin Cresswell
topic_2.text: Tollmere pays for it by the cartload and calls it Lantern Row green and charges four times. That is not stealing. That is Tollmere. — My grandmother's grandmother made it for a Sayer who was sick of fish, and the Sayer wrote it down, and now it is in a book in the Spire with somebody else's name on it. I do not mind. Cress does not care who is named for it. I care a little.

bye.speaker: Lin Cresswell
bye.text: Take a bunch. It is the second bed's, which is to say not quite right, and still better than anything the city will sell you.

q_the_top_bed_offer.speaker: Lin Cresswell
q_the_top_bed_offer.text: Will you. It is the water, the chalk or the Toll, and I can taste the first, and I can see the second, and the third I will leave to people who like being frightened. — The stream is low. It has never been low in spring. Walk up to the Cress Bridge and count the coins in the joints; there should be one in every joint, and there is always one in every joint, because nobody would dream of taking one.

choices.text: I'll walk up to the bridge.
Not now.

q_the_top_bed_accept.speaker: Lin Cresswell
q_the_top_bed_accept.text: Count them. If a joint is empty, somebody dreamed. — And do not eat the cress on the way. Not the top bed. It will not hurt you. It will not do anything, which is worse.

q_the_top_bed_decide_put_them_back.speaker: Lin Cresswell
q_the_top_bed_decide_put_them_back.text: Every coin, in its own joint, with a hammer and an apology. I will come with you and hold the lantern. — It is not superstition. It is manners.

q_the_top_bed_decide_to_the_toll_house.speaker: Lin Cresswell
q_the_top_bed_decide_to_the_toll_house.text: The Guild. — Well, it is lost coin, and they do have a box. The water will not see a mark of it and the Guild will write it down, which is the nearest thing Tollmere has to a prayer.

q_the_top_bed_decide_keep_them.speaker: Lin Cresswell
q_the_top_bed_decide_keep_them.text: It already has. — Keep them, then. You did the walking. I will wedge my own in, one a day, and we shall see whose coin the Cressbourne likes better.

q_the_top_bed_decide.speaker: Lin Cresswell
q_the_top_bed_decide.text: Robbing the water. — A Tollmere cutpurse. Of course a Tollmere cutpurse. Thirty-one coins, and the Cressbourne sulks like a cousin. And the kilns' lime grey all the way down, so the city's white walls will come up grey next and they will blame the Vale. — It is your purse now. What is it for?

choices.text: Back into the bridge, every coin.
The Guild has a box for lost coin at the Stride's Foot.
I'll keep them. The water will not miss them.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Lin Cresswell
work_going.text: Not in my beds. What the Vale wants doing besides, I can tell you. It is not much, and it pays.

greetings.text: The top bed is green at the edges. It tastes of chalk again, and a little of cold iron, and a little of somebody's pocket, which I am choosing not to think about.
Still grey. I have put a coin in the bridge every morning. The water has not said anything. Water does not.
The Guild sent me a paper for thirty-one coins, received, with a seal. The water has never had a paper before. The top bed is still grey, but it is grey in writing now.

notes: The one voice of Fallowfold (hearthvale), written with the atlas: A ewe came back from the south pasture grey to the skin and will not go into the pond; the shepherd wants her named, and does not know by whom.

greet.speaker: Gil Fallow
greet.text: Hush a moment. — Clover, Bramble, Nutmeg, Wren. — There. Fallow. Gil. You can talk now; they are in.

hub.speaker: Gil Fallow
hub.text: What do you need?

choices.text: Why graze so near the ash?
Tell me about the grey ewe.
I'll find out who else has to say Thistle's name.
The new counts on the waystone are a shepherd's. Four strokes and a bar.
Who says Thistle's name, then?
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Gil Fallow
topic_1.text: The grass is sweeter where it is poorer, which nobody believes until they taste the mutton. And somebody has to; a down that is not grazed goes to scrub, and scrub goes to nobody's, and a place that is nobody's is halfway to quiet. — The grey comes over the down on a south wind like a fine flour. We wash it out of the fleeces in the pond. The pond has never been dry. I would like it understood that I count on that.

topic_2.speaker: Gil Fallow
topic_2.text: Thistle. Four years old, twin lambs twice. She came in last week grey to the skin under the fleece, eyes and all, and she knows her name still, she comes to it, but she will not go into the pond, and she will not come past the fold gate, and she stands at the south wall looking down at the heath as if somebody had called her. — The Vale says a thing is kept by being named. She has a name. I would like to know who else has to say it.

bye.speaker: Gil Fallow
bye.text: If you pass the Rest, tell them Fallowfold's in and counted. They like to hear it, and I like them to.

q_thistle_offer.speaker: Gil Fallow
q_thistle_offer.text: She stands at the south wall all day. At dusk she puts her head up as if she is counting something, and then she lies down. — The pasture runs down to the Ninth Waystone. I have not gone past it since I was twelve. I do not intend to start now, and I would be glad if somebody else did.

choices.text: I'll walk the pasture to the waystone.
Not now.

q_thistle_accept.speaker: Gil Fallow
q_thistle_accept.text: Past the thistles and down. You will know the stone; the pilgrims have worn a seat in it. — Look at what is cut on it. The Order counts bells there. I would like to know what else is being counted.

q_thistle_whose_hand.speaker: Gil Fallow
q_thistle_whose_hand.text: ...Show me. — The bar slants. — My father cut them like that. He said a straight bar was for men who did not have to count in the rain. He walked south the spring I was twenty, to see how far the sweet grass went, and the Order wrote him down as gone on, and I have been a shepherd whose father is a line in a book ever since. — He is counting a flock down there. And she can hear him.

q_thistle_decide_keep_her.speaker: Gil Fallow
q_thistle_decide_keep_her.text: All of us, then, and loud. If he can hear it down there, good. Let him know who has her.

q_thistle_decide_let_her_go.speaker: Gil Fallow
q_thistle_decide_let_her_go.text: ...Four strokes and a bar. — I will open it at dusk, when she lifts her head. I will not watch her go. I will count the flock after, as I always do, and I will count one fewer, and it will be right.

q_thistle_decide_read_his_name.speaker: Gil Fallow
q_thistle_decide_read_his_name.text: Read again. — They read him once and he did not stop. Perhaps once is not enough for a Fallow; we were never quick. Go up to the rim, to Greywatch, and have them read it slow.

q_thistle_decide.speaker: Gil Fallow
q_thistle_decide.text: The Vale says a thing is kept by being named. She has a name, and I say it, and so does every child in the fold. And now somebody else is counting. — You have been down there. You say.

choices.text: We say it. All of us, at the pond, until she goes in.
Open the gate. She is going to him.
Have the Order read his name again, so he stops counting.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Gil Fallow
work_going.text: Not with the flock; they know me. But there is this, if you want it.

greetings.text: She went in on the fourth night. She is still grey. She is also still in the pond every morning, which is more than can be said for most of them.
The counts on the waystone went up by one last week. I cut one on the gate. That is all there is to say.

They read Aldo slow at Greywatch, the whole name and the fold after it. The counts on the waystone stopped at four strokes and a bar. Thistle still lifts her head at dusk. Then she puts it down again.

notes: The one voice of Bramcombe (hearthvale), written with the atlas: Every tally in the combe is one sheep short every morning, and no sheep is missing.

greet.speaker: Pell Brambling
greet.text: Brambling. Pell. Maud's brother; yes, the one who stayed; no, I do not regret it; yes, she asks. Mind the wash, it is deeper than it looks and the oak pipe is a liar about how fast it fills.

hub.speaker: Pell Brambling
hub.text: What is it? I have tallies to cut.

choices.text: What are the tally-sticks in every doorway?
What does your sister say about it?
Is Bramcombe old?
The sticks are one short. I'll find the sheep.
The extra sheep in the Pinfold has the old Bramcombe mark.
It is your flock's wether. What do we do?
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Pell Brambling
topic_1.text: Every house in the combe keeps its own count and I keep the combe's, and at shearing the sticks are laid side by side on the wash-house table, and they agree, and we drink. — Since spring they agree, and they are all one short. Every one. Every morning. I have counted the sheep in the fold with my own mouth and there are exactly as many as there should be. The sticks say one fewer. Nobody has cut a notch wrong; I checked every knife.

topic_2.speaker: Pell Brambling
topic_2.text: Maud says it is the Toll humming and I should come to Merrowby for a week and eat properly. Maud says everything is the Toll humming and I should eat properly. — She may be right. She usually is, which is why I live up a combe.

topic_3.speaker: Pell Brambling
topic_3.text: Older than Merrowby, by the sticks. There is a tally in the wash-house beam that nobody can read, cut before the Toll fell, and it is one short too.

bye.speaker: Pell Brambling
bye.text: Go gently on the down. The sheep are counted, even if the sticks disagree.

q_one_short_offer.speaker: Pell Brambling
q_one_short_offer.text: There is no sheep to find. That is the whole trouble. — Every stick, every morning, one short, and I count the fold with my mouth and it is right. Maud says come to Merrowby and eat properly. — The hayward in Merrowby pens the Vale's strays at the Pinfold on the Eastway. If a sheep of ours is anywhere it is there, and if it is not there it is nowhere, and I would like to know which.

choices.text: I'll look in the Pinfold.
Not now.

q_one_short_accept.speaker: Pell Brambling
q_one_short_accept.text: Read his book. He writes down everything, the hayward; it is the only thing he and the Wardens have in common. — Do not ring the bell. That is for the owner. It would be a lie, from you.

q_one_short_the_old_mark.speaker: Pell Brambling
q_one_short_the_old_mark.text: A notch under and a notch over. — That is the beam. That is the flock that was on the down before the bell came down, and every one of them two hundred years dead. — And one of them is standing in a pound in the Vale with nobody to pay his penny, and our sticks know. Of course they know. A tally is only a thing you say with a knife.

q_one_short_decide_claim_it.speaker: Pell Brambling
q_one_short_decide_claim_it.text: My penny, then, and my bell, and I will walk him up the Eastway myself with the dog. The sticks will come right. I do not know what the beam will do. I am not sure I want to.

q_one_short_decide_leave_it.speaker: Pell Brambling
q_one_short_decide_leave_it.text: The hayward's. — Yes. It is not ours to pay for a flock two hundred years under the chalk. I will stop counting the beam. I will not stop hearing it.

q_one_short_decide_to_the_lambing_fold.speaker: Pell Brambling
q_one_short_decide_to_the_lambing_fold.text: To the ewe that belongs to nobody. — A nobody's ewe and a nobody's wether. That is a flock. Go on, then. I will not come. Somebody has to count this one.

q_one_short_decide.speaker: Pell Brambling
q_one_short_decide.text: Our flock's. The combe's oldest count, and one short. — A beast nobody names goes quiet, the Vale says, and that is for villages, but I have kept sheep forty years and I have never seen why it should not be for sheep too.

choices.text: Pay the penny. Ring the bell. Walk him home.
Leave him. He is the hayward's now.
Drive him up to the grey lamb's ewe on Bram Down.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Pell Brambling
work_going.text: I keep the count, and the count says there is work. Here it is, counted.

greetings.text: The sticks agree and they are right. The beam is still one short. I have decided that is the beam's affair.
The hayward's wether is still in the Pinfold, eating the parish's grass at the parish's cost. He looks up when the Bramcombe cart goes by. So do I.
A carter saw two grey sheep on Bram Down at lambing, a ewe and a wether, grazing into the wind. The sticks come right now. I do not go up to count them.

notes: The one voice of Rookdown (hearthvale), written with the atlas: The grey patch on the green has reached the well: half the village wants to leave and half says leaving is how a village goes quiet, and they want somebody from outside to say which half is right.

greet.speaker: Tor Rookwright
greet.text: Rookwright. Tor. Reeve, for my sins, which are not many, which is why they chose me. Mind the grey on the green; do not walk on it. It does not do anything. It is simply not a place you should put your feet.

hub.speaker: Tor Rookwright
hub.text: Say it, then.

choices.text: Tell me about the grey on the green.
Why won't the rooks fly south?
Is there anything past the Brow?
You wanted somebody from outside to say which half is right.
I've seen the field and the cliff.
Has anyone seen your warrener?
He went into Tallow Barrow, after the ringing.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Tor Rookwright
topic_1.text: It came up in the Quiet Villages years as a patch the size of a door. It is the size of a threshing floor now. I measure it every Tollday and chalk the figure on the bell-post, and the village stands round the post and argues, and the arguing is the most talking Rookdown does, and I have wondered whether that is not the point of the patch. — This week it touched the well. The water is still sweet. Half of them want to take the carts to Bramcombe before it is not. Half say that is exactly how a village goes quiet. I do not know which half is right and I am the reeve.

topic_2.speaker: Tor Rookwright
topic_2.text: They fly north, east and west all day, and at the south edge of the elms they turn back as if they had struck glass. They have done it since before my grandfather. I have watched them try. — I think they know something we would rather not, and I think it is kind of them not to go and look.

topic_3.speaker: Tor Rookwright
topic_3.text: The cliff, and then the Hush. You can see it from the Hushwatch stones on a clear evening, grey as a slate, and the Vale walks up to look at it and goes home grateful. We live next to it. We are not grateful. We are simply here.

bye.speaker: Tor Rookwright
bye.text: If you are going east, keep north of the elms. The rooks will tell you where south is. Listen to them.

q_the_grey_on_the_green_offer.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_grey_on_the_green_offer.text: I did, and I am ashamed of it, and I have not changed my mind. — Half of them say take the carts to Bramcombe before the well turns. Half say leaving is how a village goes quiet, and they are not wrong either; I have read the Roll. I am the reeve and I cannot say, because whichever half I say, the other half is my cousins. — Go and look at what leaving looks like. The Last Field, south on the Brow. Then look at what staying looks like, which is the cliff. Then come and stand at the post.

choices.text: I'll go and look.
Not now.

q_the_grey_on_the_green_accept.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_grey_on_the_green_accept.text: The Last Field first. The Southcotes left their plough in it. It is still there. Something is still using it.

q_the_grey_on_the_green_decide_stay.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_grey_on_the_green_decide_stay.text: Every name, every Tollday, louder than the grey. — That is the Vale's answer and it is a good one, and it will cost us the well, or it will not. I will chalk it up.

q_the_grey_on_the_green_decide_go.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_grey_on_the_green_decide_go.text: Go. — A village is its people. I have said that to myself for a month and never once aloud. I will say it at the post, and my cousins will not speak to me for a year, and then they will, in Bramcombe.

q_the_grey_on_the_green_decide_turn_the_.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_grey_on_the_green_decide_turn_the_.text: Turn her back. — She drowned facing it; she can watch it. And if she turns round again, we will know something the beacon does not. That is a Rookdown answer. It is not an answer. We shall like it very much.

q_the_grey_on_the_green_decide.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_grey_on_the_green_decide.text: Then say it at the post, not to me. — No. Say it to me first, so I can hear how it sounds before they do. My great-aunt's stone has turned to face us. The beacon was lit twice. The well is sweet today. Say.

choices.text: Stay, and say every name at the post each Tollday.
Go to Bramcombe while the water is sweet.
Turn her stone back to the Hush. Let the drowned watch for you.
Let me think on it.

q_the_warreners_burrow_offer.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_warreners_burrow_offer.text: Not since the Long Table. — He was never much for company; a warrener is a man who has chosen rabbits. But he comes down for bread on Tallowdays, and he has not, and the boy I sent to feed his ferrets came back white and will not say why except that the rabbits are leaving. — His camp is up under the Thornmarch in the gorse. Go up.

choices.text: I'll go up to his camp.
Not now.

q_the_warreners_burrow_accept.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_warreners_burrow_accept.text: Take bread. If he is there, he will want it, and if he is not, the ferrets will.

q_the_warreners_burrow_decide_wall_it.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_warreners_burrow_decide_wall_it.text: Wall it, with chalk and flint and a Warden watching. If he wants to come out, he can knock. They say the barrow listens.

q_the_warreners_burrow_decide_leave_it.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_warreners_burrow_decide_leave_it.text: His own feet. — Yes. I will leave bread on the stone at the gap on Tallowdays, and I will not say who it is for.

q_the_warreners_burrow_decide_ferrets_to.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_warreners_burrow_decide_ferrets_to.text: Tamwick's tanners know a boy who can whistle a ferret. The down will have a warrener by harvest, and he will stay out of the barrow, because I will tell him about this one.

q_the_warreners_burrow_decide.speaker: Tor Rookwright
q_the_warreners_burrow_decide.text: Into the barrow. — The Tollmere diggers came out of it without their spades in 1012 and it walled itself up behind them. And now it has a door in it and a warrener through it. — What do I do with a door, then? I am a reeve. I keep the green, the well, the rookery and the peace. Nobody told me about the down.

choices.text: Wall it up again.
Leave it. He chose to go.
Give his ferrets to Tamwick. The down needs a warrener.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Tor Rookwright
work_going.text: A reeve knows what wants doing. This is the week's, and none of it is on the green.

greetings.text: Every name, every Tollday. The patch is the same size this week. It has never been the same size two weeks running. I have chalked that up too, with a line under it.
Long Table, the carts go. The rooks will stay. I have asked them. They did not answer, which is a rook's yes.
My great-aunt faces the Hush again. The patch came to the foot of the cliff in the frost and stopped there, as if somebody had told it to. We have agreed not to say who.
The gap is walled, chalk and flint, with a Warden's mark on it. Nobody has knocked. The Warden who watches it says the wall is warm in the mornings. I have told her to stop touching it.
The bread I leave at the gap on Tallowdays is gone by Hushday. Rabbits, I tell the green. The rabbits on the down have never been so fat, and not one of them will go near the barrow.
The Tamwick boy whistles his ferrets on the down every morning and keeps well south of the barrow. I told him why. He has the sense to be frightened, which is more than his master had.

notes: The one voice of Hazelcombe (hearthvale), written with the atlas: The Wardens have ordered a mile of hurdles for new pens on the grey border, and the weavers want to know what the pens are for before they weave them.

greet.speaker: Tam Withy
greet.text: Withy. Tam. Hold that end — no, the other end. There. You have just helped make a hurdle and it will go to a fold on the downs and outlast us both.

hub.speaker: Tam Withy
hub.text: Go on, then, while my hands are busy.

choices.text: What are the Wardens' new pens for?
What is it like, trading with the Woodfolk?
Why the odd rod in every hurdle?
I'll find out what the pens are for.
The pens are for the grey beasts. The Wold won't sell rods for them.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Tam Withy
topic_1.text: A mile of hurdles, ordered from the Rest, to be carted to the border above the ash and set in pens. Not folds: pens, with no gate, the order says, just a door you can bar from the outside. — I have woven hurdles for folds and for pens and for a Long Table dance floor once, and I have never woven for a pen with no gate. I have asked the Wardens what goes in them and they have said something that comes back grey, and I have not woven a rod since.

topic_2.speaker: Tam Withy
topic_2.text: Like trading with a wall that has opinions. They cut the rods on a seven-year round and sell me exactly what the round gives and not a rod over, and when I asked once for more they looked at me the way you look at a man who has asked for more mother. — They are right, mostly. It is very tiresome.

topic_3.speaker: Tam Withy
topic_3.text: So I can find my work. A hurdle goes out of this yard and into a fold and the fold goes to a son and then to a stranger, and the hurdle is still standing, and somebody has to know who made it. I know. That is enough knowing for a hurdle.

bye.speaker: Tam Withy
bye.text: Mind the rod stacks on your way out. They are taller than they are steady, like most of us.

q_pens_with_no_gate_offer.speaker: Tam Withy
q_pens_with_no_gate_offer.text: Would you. — I have asked the Wardens and they said something that comes back grey, and a Warden who says something instead of a thing has not decided whether to lie. And the Woodfolk have stopped selling me rods, which they have not done since the year my father sold them a hurdle he had not made. — Ask at the Rest. Ask plainly. Sergeant Dole will answer a plain question, it is the only kind he can hear.

choices.text: I'll ask at the Rest.
Not now.

q_pens_with_no_gate_accept.speaker: Tam Withy
q_pens_with_no_gate_accept.text: And then ask the Wold. I cannot; they look at me like a man asking for more mother. They may look at you like somebody else's mother, which is better.

q_pens_with_no_gate_decide_as_ordered.speaker: Tam Withy
q_pens_with_no_gate_decide_as_ordered.text: As ordered. — I will buy the rods from the Vale's own copses at twice the price and weave a worse hurdle with them, and I will know it every time I look at the pens, and the Wardens will not.

q_pens_with_no_gate_decide_a_gate_south.speaker: Tam Withy
q_pens_with_no_gate_decide_a_gate_south.text: A gate on the grey side, and the door on the Vale side barred. — That is a hurdle. That is a hurdle a Woodfolk could sell me a rod for, too. I will take it to Aggie myself, with a jug.

q_pens_with_no_gate_decide_refuse.speaker: Tam Withy
q_pens_with_no_gate_decide_refuse.text: Not my work. — I will write to the Rest and tell them so, and they will find another weaver, and he will be a worse one, and the pens will fall down the first winter. There is some comfort in that. Not much.

q_pens_with_no_gate_decide.speaker: Tam Withy
q_pens_with_no_gate_decide.text: Beasts. — And whatever else comes back. I heard the after-a-while in it too, you know; Dole cannot keep a pause out of his voice to save his life. — And Aggie says no, because it is custom, and it is always custom with Aggie when she means it, and when she does not it is the price. — I have to weave something. Tell me what.

choices.text: Weave them as ordered.
Put a gate in the south side. Let them walk back down.
Refuse. It is not your work.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Tam Withy
work_going.text: I weave. Other people want things carried and killed, and they will pay you for it. This is what they want.

greetings.text: Aggie sold me rods. At her price, not mine, and she came to see the gates herself. She said they would do. That is the most any Woodfolk has ever said about anything I made.
The pens are up, as ordered, of Vale rods at twice the price. The Wardens came and said they were good pens. They are not. I have stopped looking at them, which comes to the same thing.
The Rest found another weaver, a Tollmere man with a rule and no hands. His pens lean already. The first beast will walk straight through them, and I will be sorry, and I will not be wrong.

notes: The one voice of The Hare and Hurdle (hearthvale), written with the atlas: The innkeeper's board of who owes whom a drink has one debt on it, in chalk that will not rub off, owed to a man nobody can remember.

greet.speaker: Cal Merriweather
greet.text: Welcome to the Hare. Merriweather, Cal, keeper. There is ale, there is cider from Tamwick if Bessa has been through, and there is a skittle alley, and if you lose at it you paint the sign.

hub.speaker: Cal Merriweather
hub.text: What'll it be?

choices.text: What is the debt on the board that will not rub off?
Who comes through the Hare?
Who paints the sign?
I'll find your Dunn.
Your Dunn was Dunnet Hale, a keeper of Hound Watch.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Cal Merriweather
topic_1.text: Top left. 'One to Dunn, from the Hare.' My aunt's hand, I think; the chalk is hers. It will not rub off. I have tried water, vinegar and a Sayer. — Nobody on the downs knows a Dunn. The Roll has no Dunn. Pellam in Merrowby does not know a Dunn, and Pellam knows everybody who ever owed anybody. The house owes a man a drink and the man is nowhere, and I would very much like to pay it.

topic_2.speaker: Cal Merriweather
topic_2.text: Drovers taking Bram Down's lambs to Merrowby market, carters with flint from the Pits, Wardens coming off the border tower shifts with the look of men who have been staring at grey for nine days. Rookdown folk, lately, with their carts loaded and their faces set, going north, and then coming back again two days later, not saying anything. — I pour for all of them. The Hare is a hurdle: it keeps the weather out, that is all.

topic_3.speaker: Cal Merriweather
topic_3.text: Whoever loses at skittles on Long Table night. The hare has been painted by a Warden, a Sayer, a knight of the Order and once by Bessa Tamwick, who lost on purpose because she said the last hare looked like it was apologising.

bye.speaker: Cal Merriweather
bye.text: Mind the step on the way out; it's where the hare lands.

q_one_to_dunn_offer.speaker: Cal Merriweather
q_one_to_dunn_offer.text: Find him and I will pour him the best in the house and stand him a second for his trouble, and then I will wipe that board with a clear heart for the first time in twenty years. — My aunt kept the board honest and she wrote that line and she never told me who he was, and I have never known her to write a debt she did not mean. — The Wardens off the towers drink here. Start with Hound Watch, over the down. Its keepers have the look.

choices.text: I'll ask at Hound Watch.
Not now.

q_one_to_dunn_accept.speaker: Cal Merriweather
q_one_to_dunn_accept.text: Tell the keeper the Hare sent you. He will want to know if his slate is clean. It is not.

q_one_to_dunn_decide_pour_it.speaker: Cal Merriweather
q_one_to_dunn_decide_pour_it.text: Facing the Choir, the best in the house, and then the cup comes home and goes on the shelf behind the bar, where it should have been. I will wipe the board myself.

q_one_to_dunn_decide_write_his_name.speaker: Cal Merriweather
q_one_to_dunn_decide_write_his_name.text: Dunnet Hale, under One to Dunn, in my chalk under hers. — Let the drovers ask. I will tell them. A man is owed a drink, and the Hare knows who.

q_one_to_dunn_decide_tell_the_rest.speaker: Cal Merriweather
q_one_to_dunn_decide_tell_the_rest.text: The Rest scraped him off a board so that nobody would follow him down. — I understand it. I will tell them anyway. A Warden who is owed a drink is still a Warden.

q_one_to_dunn_decide.speaker: Cal Merriweather
q_one_to_dunn_decide.text: Dunnet Hale. — My aunt knew him, then. She would have. She knew every Warden who ever came off a tower with that look. And he went down to the Choir, and she wrote him a drink, and she carried a cup to the Last Look and kept it filled, and she never said. — The house owes him. Tell me how the house pays.

choices.text: Pour it at the Last Look, facing the Choir, and bring the cup home.
Write his name under the debt.
Tell the Rest. They took his name off.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Cal Merriweather
work_going.text: The drovers leave word at the bar of what wants doing on the downs. This is what they left.

greetings.text: The board's clean. First time in twenty years. I keep looking at the top left corner like a tongue at a gap.
Dunnet Hale. The drovers ask, and I tell them, and they drink to him. He is the best-drunk-to man on the downs.
A Warden came in from the Rest with a coin for One to Dunn and would not drink it himself. It stands on the bar under the board, poured. Nobody touches it. It is the best-kept glass in the house.

notes: The one voice of The Last Camp (cinderlea), written with the atlas: A pilgrim who has waited three years asks for the one thing she has not been able to find out: whether anybody would say her name if she stayed.

greet.speaker: Nella Candlewright
greet.text: Sit if you like. Nobody here will ask you anything. That is the whole of the camp: a rim, a fire, and nobody asking.

hub.speaker: Nella Candlewright
hub.text: You may ask me, though. You look like you would.

choices.text: Why haven't you gone on?
Why only half a candle?
You want to know whether anybody would say your name.
Merrowby says your name. So does the knight at Greywatch, every night.
I am ready to walk when you are.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Nella Candlewright
topic_1.text: I do not know. That is the honest answer and I have had three years to find a better one. — I walked down from Merrowby with my mind made up and I reached this rim and sat down to rest, and the next morning I made a candle, and I have made one every evening since. The Order says the ones who wait are not stopped, only slow. I think I am waiting to find out whether anybody would say my name if I stayed. Nobody here says names. It is the rule.

topic_2.speaker: Nella Candlewright
topic_2.text: A whole one is a night. Half is a promise to come back and finish it. I have a tent full of half-candles. The knights take them to the chapter-house and burn the other halves on Candle Night, and the chapter-house is the brightest it has been in a hundred years, they tell me, and that is the only thing I know I have done since I sat down.

bye.speaker: Nella Candlewright
bye.text: Go gently on the rim. The Hush does not pull. It simply waits, like me.

q_would_anybody_say_it_offer.speaker: Nella Candlewright
q_would_anybody_say_it_offer.text: Nobody here says names; it is the rule, and I made it mine the day I sat down. — I walked down from Merrowby with my mind made up and reached this rim and rested, and made a candle in the morning, and have made one every evening since. The Order says the ones who wait are not stopped, only slow. I think I am waiting to find out whether anybody would say my name if I stayed. — I cannot ask. If I walk north to ask, I have answered. You could ask. Ask Maud Brambling. She knows everything and says half of it, and the half is always true.

choices.text: I'll ask in Merrowby.
Not now.

q_would_anybody_say_it_accept.speaker: Nella Candlewright
q_would_anybody_say_it_accept.text: Do not tell her I sent you. — Tell her anyway. She will know. She always knows who sent people.

q_would_anybody_say_it_decide_stay.speaker: Nella Candlewright
q_would_anybody_say_it_decide_stay.text: Stay, and be said. — Then this is not waiting any more. It is living on a rim and making candles, which is a thing a person can do on purpose. I will do it on purpose.

q_would_anybody_say_it_decide_go_home.speaker: Nella Candlewright
q_would_anybody_say_it_decide_go_home.text: Home. — As far as the first clean water, and then I shall see whether my legs remember the rest. Give me the evening to put out the last candle. Then we will walk.

q_would_anybody_say_it_decide_go_on.speaker: Nella Candlewright
q_would_anybody_say_it_decide_go_on.text: Read at the stones, every night, by a knight who knows my candles. — Then I can go. I have been afraid of going unsaid, and I will not be. Thank you. I will leave the tent to whoever sits down next.

q_would_anybody_say_it_decide.speaker: Nella Candlewright
q_would_anybody_say_it_decide.text: Every night. — On no roll, because I am not gone, only slow. — And my half-candle at the Cross, burning since midsummer and not shorter. — I put that there on my way south. I had forgotten. I had not forgotten. — Three years. Tell me what to do with it, and I will do it, because I have not been able to decide anything since I sat down, and I am very tired of this rim.

choices.text: Stay. You're said.
Go home and finish the candle. I'll walk with you.
Go on south. You'll be read.
Let me think on it.

q_would_anybody_say_it_walk_her_home.speaker: Nella Candlewright
q_would_anybody_say_it_walk_her_home.text: Then we go. — The last candle is out. I have left the tent standing for whoever sits down next; somebody always does. Walk on my left. I have not walked north in three years, and I keep wanting to turn round.

work_going.speaker: Nella Candlewright
work_going.text: Nothing here wants doing but candles. The knights leave word of the rest when they come for them. Here it is.

greetings.text: Sit, if you like. — You may say my name. I will allow it. Just the once.
The candle at the Cross burned down the night I came home. I have made a new one for the niche. Merrowby buys my candles again and complains about the price, which is how I know I am home.

notes: The one voice of The West Walk (cinderlea), written with the atlas: Someone has been working Ossel's forge at night, and what they are making is a bell-bearer's clapper.

greet.speaker: Merrit Ash
greet.text: Merrit Ash, the west walk. You are on it. It goes from the White Wood to where the reeds go grey, and back, and I have walked it four thousand times, and it is exactly as long as it was the first night.

hub.speaker: Merrit Ash
hub.text: Ask. I have the day to sleep and nobody to say anything to.

choices.text: Why is the wall made of doors?
Whose forge is it?
What is at the end of the west walk?
Somebody's working Ossel's forge at night.
It comes through the North Gate at night, smelling of your trough.
Pellam Ashcombe asks you to read him the doors.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Merrit Ash
topic_1.text: Ashcombe's. The hamlet went quiet in the Ash Winter, before Greyfold, and nobody remembers it at all, which is worse. The Order took the doors off their hinges so the houses would not be kept shut on nothing, and built the post out of them. — I was a lock-maker. They are good doors. Every one of them was shut by somebody who meant to open it again.

topic_2.speaker: Merrit Ash
topic_2.text: Ossel's. Smith's daughter, of Gullhithe. She kept the forge and the west walk both, and in the autumn of 1019 she went out to bring in a bell-bearer's clapper and did not. We use her quench; the water in the trough has been changed every week since. The forge has not been lit. — It has been lit, lately. Three nights. Somebody is working a clapper on her anvil, and I have come back from the round each time to find it warm and nobody here.

topic_3.speaker: Merrit Ash
topic_3.text: The reeds, going grey. The marsh folk cut them at Nauvissa and sell them to us for wicks. Past that, the ash runs into the water and you cannot tell which is which. I turn round there. The Vigil Book says to keep the ring, and the ring is wherever you turn round.

bye.speaker: Merrit Ash
bye.text: Walk with somebody, if you walk west. It is not dangerous. It is simply better with somebody.

q_ossels_forge_offer.speaker: Merrit Ash
q_ossels_forge_offer.text: Three nights, and a clapper on the anvil, warm, and nobody. — Ossel kept this forge and the walk both. Smith's daughter, of Gullhithe; she could shoe a horse and ring a bell and walk the round in one night and not once complain. In the autumn of nineteen she went out to bring in a bell-bearer's clapper and did not. We use her trough. We change the water every week. We have not lit the forge. — Look at what is on the anvil. I have not touched it. I was a lock-maker; I know better than to touch another hand's work while it is warm.

choices.text: I'll look at the anvil.
Not now.

q_ossels_forge_accept.speaker: Merrit Ash
q_ossels_forge_accept.text: Then the pit. The bell-bearers dig at night. — And then the north gate. Something walks through it at the same hour every night, and I have been meaning to stand there and see for eleven years, and I have not, because I walk the round.

q_ossels_forge_decide_quench_it.speaker: Merrit Ash
q_ossels_forge_decide_quench_it.text: Cold, in her trough, and on the wall with the doors, unrung. A clapper that is never swung is a promise kept by not keeping it. I understand those. I sleep behind forty of them.

q_ossels_forge_decide_let_her_finish.speaker: Merrit Ash
q_ossels_forge_decide_let_her_finish.text: Back on the anvil, and the forge laid, and the trough fresh. — If a bell rings from the pit one night I will stand at the gate and count it. That is all the Order asks: that it is counted.

q_ossels_forge_decide_bury_it.speaker: Merrit Ash
q_ossels_forge_decide_bury_it.text: In the pit, deep, with the broken bells. — The Order buried them so nobody would ring a broken one. I will bury it myself, with the bound clapper, and not tell anyone where.

q_ossels_forge_decide.speaker: Merrit Ash
q_ossels_forge_decide.text: Of the trough. — Of Ossel's trough. — Something that walks through the north gate carrying something heavy and smells of a quench nobody has used since nineteen, working a clapper for a dug-up bell. — I will not say her name. The Order says a name when it knows. Tell me what to do with the clapper.

choices.text: Quench it cold and hang it on the door-wall.
Put it back and let her finish it.
Bury it in the pit with the bells nobody should ring.
Let me think on it.

q_ashcombe_on_the_roll_the_doors.speaker: Merrit Ash
q_ashcombe_on_the_roll_the_doors.text: Ashcombe's doors, name by name. — I know them by the hand, not the reading; I was a lock-maker. Nineteen houses. Ashcombe-Mill, over the mill-race door with the iron studs. Hobb's Cross. The Two Wells. The Weaver's. Cold Harbour, which was a joke; it is the warmest door. And on round to the Widow's End, which has a lock on it I made the key for myself, eleven years ago, so that I would have something to open. — Tell him that. Tell him the doors were every one shut by somebody who meant to open them again.

work_going.speaker: Merrit Ash
work_going.text: The Walk posts its work at the gate. I will read it to you; my eyes are better than the board's paint.

greetings.text: The clapper hangs cold on the door-wall with the forty doors, unrung. Nothing has come through the North Gate since. The trough is dry. I miss the smell of it, which I will not say to the knights.
The forge is laid and the trough fresh every evening. Three nights ago a bell rang once from the Bell Pit. I stood at the gate and counted it. One. The Order asks that it is counted.

It is buried with the broken bells and I am the only one who knows where. Something walked the North Gate twice more, heavier each time, and then stopped. I sleep behind forty doors and a secret. That is one too many.

notes: The one voice of Stride's Foot (brightwater), written with the atlas: One traveller a week is entered in the toll-ledger going out to the city and never coming back, always in the same hand, and the hand is not a clerk's.

greet.speaker: Corin Stilyard
greet.text: Stilyard, senior clerk, Stride's Foot. Everything that goes to the city on wheels is weighed here and priced, and you are not on wheels, so you are free, which is the only free thing between here and the Spire.

hub.speaker: Corin Stilyard
hub.text: State your business. Briefly; there is a cart.

choices.text: What is odd about the ledger?
How much is the toll?
I'll find out whose hand is in your ledger.
They all went out to the city and were never said at home again.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Corin Stilyard
topic_1.text: Nothing is odd about my ledger. My ledger is correct. — One entry a week is not mine. A traveller, on foot, going out along the Stride toward the city, weight of pack given, name given, and the same hand every time, a hand like a child copying letters. And nobody of that name comes back through the Foot, ever, and nobody at the city end has them going in. Nineteen entries since winter. I have sat up with the book. The page is blank when I close it and written when I open it, and I would like it to stop, or to be paid for it.

topic_2.speaker: Corin Stilyard
topic_2.text: By weight and by kind, per the Charter of 712 as amended forty-one times, and I will not recite the amendments unless you have an afternoon and a grievance. Foot traffic is free. That is the forty-second amendment, and I voted against it, and I was right, and it is still free.

bye.speaker: Corin Stilyard
bye.text: Mind the lamps on the Stride at dusk. They light one after the other and it is a very beautiful thing and people walk into the water watching it.

q_the_same_hand_offer.speaker: Corin Stilyard
q_the_same_hand_offer.text: Please. — I have sat up with the book three nights running. I close it, blank; I blink; it is written. Nineteen names since winter, a traveller a week, on foot, going out. Nobody of those names comes back through the Foot, and the city clerks have none of them going in. — There is a man on the bench at the Larkmouth Bridge every night until dawn. I do not like to ask him things; he is Vale, and they have long silences. You may be better at it. Take the page. I have cut it out; the Guild will want to know why and I will tell them it was a correction.

choices.text: I'll sit with the man on the bench.
Not now.

q_the_same_hand_accept.speaker: Corin Stilyard
q_the_same_hand_accept.text: Foot traffic is free, you know. It is the forty-second amendment. I voted against it. — I was wrong. I have never said that about an amendment before.

q_the_same_hand_decide_strike_them.speaker: Corin Stilyard
q_the_same_hand_decide_strike_them.text: Struck, with a ruled line and my initials, which is how a correction is made. — If they write themselves in again I shall strike them again. That is also how a correction is made.

q_the_same_hand_decide_send_word.speaker: Corin Stilyard
q_the_same_hand_decide_send_word.text: Nineteen letters. The Guild will charge me postage and I will pay it and enter it under sundries. — Hew Coomb's daughter has a room on Canal End and three children. I will write that one myself.

q_the_same_hand_decide_leave_the_book_op.speaker: Corin Stilyard
q_the_same_hand_decide_leave_the_book_op.text: Open, on the desk, with a lamp. — If something wants to keep a count of who went out along the Stride and was never said again, it may keep it in my book. It is the correct book. It is the only one there is.

q_the_same_hand_decide.speaker: Corin Stilyard
q_the_same_hand_decide.text: Eleven alive in the city and eight on the harbour roll, and every one of them written out of the book they came from, and into mine. — I am a Tallyman. A ledger is for what is owed. I do not know what this is owed. You tell me.

choices.text: Strike them. They're not tolls.
Send word home with their names.
Leave the book open and let it write.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Corin Stilyard
work_going.text: I weigh what comes in along the Stride. This is what is wanted going out, and what it pays, weighed.

greetings.text: Hew Coomb walked out along the Stride last Tollday, on foot, free. I weighed nothing. I entered him anyway. In my hand.
Nine times now I have struck the same line with my initials. The hand is patient. So am I. The Guild does not know it is paying me to have an argument.

The book lay open on the desk all night with a lamp. In the morning there were two new names in the margin, in that hand, and one of them was a Wynstead name. I lit the lamp again. It is the correct book.

notes: The one voice of Sedgehithe (brightwater), written with the atlas: The reed fringe is dying back from the shore in a straight line, as if something were drawing a rule across the water.

greet.speaker: Maudie Punt
greet.text: Punt. Maudie. Yes, really; my father had a sense of humour and a boat. Mind the bollards, they ring if you knock them, and the reeds do not like it.

hub.speaker: Maudie Punt
hub.text: Say what you came to say. The tide is not a thing on the Mere, but the light is.

choices.text: What is wrong with the reed fringe?
Why are the bollards shaped like bells?
The line in the reeds. I'll find out what's drawing it.
It's a Builders' kerb under the silt. The Mere is falling.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Maudie Punt
topic_1.text: It is going back. Not dying from the edges like weed-rot: going back in a straight line, as if somebody had laid a rule across the bay and everything west of the rule has decided it is not reed any more. The line moves a pole's length a week, toward the Eelweir. — The reedfolk at the weir say it is the Tide account come true, the water going out. The Sayers say it is a measurement error. The reeds say nothing, which in my experience is when to listen.

topic_2.speaker: Maudie Punt
topic_2.text: The Builders made them. Everything the Builders made is shaped like a bell if you look at it long enough, the Sayers say, which is either very deep or a sign that the Sayers need to look at something else. — You tie a punt to one and it hums while the punt rocks. My mother said it was the lake saying the boat's name. I have never had the heart to tell her it was the rope.

bye.speaker: Maudie Punt
bye.text: Go round by the shore path. The reeds will cut you if you go through them, and they will be right to.

q_the_ruled_line_offer.speaker: Maudie Punt
q_the_ruled_line_offer.text: Nobody is drawing it. That is what frightens the cutters; a line with nobody drawing it. — Go up the Heronry and look at it from above. The herons went west in the middle of the nesting, which herons do not do, and from the top you will see what they saw. Then go and look at the weir. Everything on this bay ends up at the weir sooner or later. Punts, eels, arguments.

choices.text: I'll climb the Heronry.
Not now.

q_the_ruled_line_accept.speaker: Maudie Punt
q_the_ruled_line_accept.text: Mind the nests; they are empty but they have opinions. — And if you meet a Sayer on the water, ask them what they are measuring. There has been one about. They do not wave.

q_the_ruled_line_decide_the_tide.speaker: Maudie Punt
q_the_ruled_line_decide_the_tide.text: The weir, then. They will sing about it, which is how the reedfolk write things down, and it will be in a round by midsummer and nobody will be able to stop singing it.

q_the_ruled_line_decide_the_circle.speaker: Maudie Punt
q_the_ruled_line_decide_the_circle.text: Twelve times. — Take the book up the hill and put it on a desk and make somebody read it out loud. Tell them a reed-cutter sent you. They will not know what that means. Tell them anyway.

q_the_ruled_line_decide_cut_to_the_line.speaker: Maudie Punt
q_the_ruled_line_decide_cut_to_the_line.text: Cut and sell. — It is what a cutter does, and I am a cutter, and the thatchers will pay. I will leave the last pole of green at the line standing. I do not know why. I will.

q_the_ruled_line_decide.speaker: Maudie Punt
q_the_ruled_line_decide.text: Falling. — My father said the Mere was resting. My mother's people say it is going out, like the Tide, and will come back. And under my reeds there is a stone kerb the Builders laid straight as a rule, and the water is going down along it like a hand along a table. — Who hears this first? Say.

choices.text: The reedfolk. It is their account.
The Circle. Their Sayer measured it twelve times.
Cut to the line and sell what you can.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Maudie Punt
work_going.text: The reed wants cutting, and I cut it. The rest of the Mere wants this.

greetings.text: The reedfolk have a round about the kerb now. The children sing it cutting, and there is a line in it about a woman who pushed her punt along the Builders' ruler. That is me. It does not scan.

A Circle Sayer came down with a pole and a boy and measured my reeds from the punt for a week. She left me a copy of the book with the line drawn in and my name spelt right. The water is still going down.
The thatchers paid well. The last pole of green still stands at the line, on its own, like somebody waiting for a ferry. I cut round it every morning.

notes: The one voice of Merrowhithe (brightwater), written with the atlas: The dry aqueduct has started to drip, and there is nothing upstream of it but Skerrow.

greet.speaker: Berrit Smoker
greet.text: Smoker. Berrit. It is not a joke, it is a trade. You will smell of oak for a day; everybody does.

hub.speaker: Berrit Smoker
hub.text: Well?

choices.text: What is the aqueduct for?
Do you have opinions about the city?
Your third arch drips. I'll find out from where.
It's the Rust Scar's water. The day it ran clear.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Berrit Smoker
topic_1.text: Nothing, for eleven hundred years. The Builders ran it down off the heights to somewhere, and it broke, and it has been dry since before the Toll fell. We hang pike in the arches and smoke them, and the arches draw like a chimney, which is the only water-work it has ever done for us. — This spring it drips. From the third arch, onto the landing, day and night. The water is cold and tastes of stone and nothing else, and there is nothing up the line of it but the Rudd Cliffs and Skerrow and snow.

topic_2.speaker: Berrit Smoker
topic_2.text: No. — That is the whole of the answer. People are always disappointed. They come up the shore from Tollmere with an argument and find a man and a lot of fish, and go home thinking Merrowhithe is simple. We are not simple. We are finished thinking about it.

bye.speaker: Berrit Smoker
bye.text: Take a pike. Wrap it well. Oak smoke is honest; it will tell the whole shore where you have been.

q_the_third_arch_offer.speaker: Berrit Smoker
q_the_third_arch_offer.text: From the heights. There is nothing else up there. — It drips cold and it tastes of stone, and I do not care about the stone, I care that I have hung fish under a dry arch for thirty-two years and I do not know what I am hanging them under now. — Walk the line of it up onto the cliff-top. The Standing Arches go on from there to Rudd Beck. If it goes further than Rudd Beck, it goes into the clans' country, and you will want a warmer coat.

choices.text: I'll walk the line of it.
Not now.

q_the_third_arch_accept.speaker: Berrit Smoker
q_the_third_arch_accept.text: Take a pike for the road. You will smell of oak for a day. Everybody does; it is not personal.

q_the_third_arch_decide_catch_it.speaker: Berrit Smoker
q_the_third_arch_decide_catch_it.text: A cask, then, a clean one, and the boy can carry it up on Tallowdays. The Rudd can name their children in it. I will send a pike with it. They will think it is a joke. It is not a joke. It is a trade.

q_the_third_arch_decide_let_it_drip.speaker: Berrit Smoker
q_the_third_arch_decide_let_it_drip.text: Eleven hundred years dry and it has found its water. — I will move the rack. The fish do not need to hang under it, and the arch does not need fish.

q_the_third_arch_decide_stop_it.speaker: Berrit Smoker
q_the_third_arch_decide_stop_it.text: Clay, then. I will do it myself, and I will not enjoy it, and the Rudd will never know, which is the worst of it. Here: the lads' wages for a week. You earned them walking.

q_the_third_arch_decide.speaker: Berrit Smoker
q_the_third_arch_decide.text: The Rudd name their children for it. — And I have been smoking pike under it. — I do not have opinions about the city, and I did not think I had any about the clans either. I find I do. You tell me what is decent. You have been up there.

choices.text: Catch it in a cask and send it up to Ruddow.
Let it drip. It has water in it again.
Pack it with clay. You need the arches dry.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Berrit Smoker
work_going.text: Work pays in fish or in marks. This pays in marks.

greetings.text: The Rudd sent a cask back down, full of honey-brew. The boy drank half of it on the road. I would have too.

The drip has made a pool under the third arch, and a heron stands in it in the mornings as if it pays rent. I moved the rack. The arch is louder than it was. I have got used to it, which I did not expect.
The third arch is dry and the pike hang straight under it. The clay went dark in a week and it stays dark. I do not stand under that one when I can help it.

notes: The one voice of Moreva (sedgemire), written with the atlas: The eel-traps have started coming up full of something that is not eels, with a lantern-maker's knot tied round it.

traps_lifted.speaker: Sauve Mor
traps_lifted.text: Nine eels and a boot. The boot's the watch's; Tella lost it here in spring chasing somebody who was lying in the reeds a yard from her. That was me. — You came down the boards like a cart. You'll learn. The fog helps; the dark helps; being low helps most. Nobody looks at the ground. They look where it's loud.

strongbox_help.speaker: Sauve Mor
strongbox_help.text: There's a pin inside that wants to sit, and a moment when it will. You'll feel it come round. Set it then and not before, and if you set it wrong the pick goes, and picks cost, so don't. — Sneak widens the moment. Practice widens the Sneak. The Tallymen widen nothing.

report_done.speaker: Sauve Mor
report_done.text: Tithe-book. Ours. And this, in the back. — A village's debt, and a word across it: unsay. Somebody's paid to have a name struck off. That's not a collector's word. That's somebody in Tollmere's word. — Take the bravo's horse. A horse with no rider is nobody's, and the only man who'd say otherwise is in the reeds with a reason not to. I'll keep her fed. In the morning, watch the courier.

courier_ask.speaker: Sauve Mor
courier_ask.text: He's got the other copy. He ought to be on the Tollmere road with it, and he's looking south, and his face has gone the colour of the fog. — My man in Gullhithe wants your page. I want to know where his is going. Go after him. Don't catch him. Just see.

greet.speaker: Sauve Mor
greet.text: Mor. Sauve. Issa at Isseva is my cousin and a liar about eels, which is the family trade as much as the trapping. Mind the traps on the boards; they are wet and they bite.

hub.speaker: Sauve Mor
hub.text: Ask slowly. The eels are listening.

choices.text: The traps are up.
How do I pick it?
The collector's satchel.
Where's the courier going?
What is coming up in the traps?
Why put the first eel back?
The knots in your traps. And the Fog Bell has stopped.
They're Mor'oul's knots. Nine lanterns under the water have none.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Sauve Mor
topic_1.text: Knots. Lantern-makers' knots, the kind they tie round a burial lantern so it floats true, and nothing inside them. A hank of indigo rush tied round nothing, in a trap that was empty of eels. Nine this month. — The lantern-makers at Saeva say every knot is somebody's. They say these were tied for lanterns that went out on the water eighty years ago, and should have come apart at sea.

topic_2.speaker: Sauve Mor
topic_2.text: Go and tell them, we say. Tell who, the children ask, and we say the other eels, so they know what they are getting into. — My grandfather said it meant the ones under the water, the drowned, so they know we are still here and still fishing and have not forgotten them. I do not say which. I put the eel back. It swims off. Somebody down there knows we are here.

bye.speaker: Sauve Mor
bye.text: Go by the boards, not the reeds. The reeds are for eels, and they know it.

q_knots_round_nothing_offer.speaker: Sauve Mor
q_knots_round_nothing_offer.text: Stopped at the third quarter, when the fog was thickest, and every boat on the channel came in by feel and swearing. — The ringer is an old man and a good one and he does not stop. I think it is the knots. Nine, and every one tied the Saeva way round a lantern that is not there. — Go out to the bell. If he is up the ladder asleep, wake him. If he is not, look at his post. He scratches everything on the post.

choices.text: I'll go out to the Fog Bell.
Not now.

q_knots_round_nothing_accept.speaker: Sauve Mor
q_knots_round_nothing_accept.text: Take the pole with the hook. The channel is shallow at the bend and there is always something in the shallows that would like to be pulled out.

q_knots_round_nothing_decide_ring_the_be.speaker: Sauve Mor
q_knots_round_nothing_decide_ring_the_be.text: Moreva rings it, then, turn about, every quarter hour while the fog is down. I will take the first night. If he comes up, he will find his bell being rung badly, and he will be furious, and I will be glad.

q_knots_round_nothing_decide_send_them_o.speaker: Sauve Mor
q_knots_round_nothing_decide_send_them_o.text: Nine new lanterns, tied with the old knots, sung out on the south channel the way it should have been done eighty years ago. Lisse Tal will know how. The Tals know how to do everything with rush and nothing with people.

q_knots_round_nothing_decide_put_them_ba.speaker: Sauve Mor
q_knots_round_nothing_decide_put_them_ba.text: Back in the traps, then, and if they come up again I will put them back again. The water has a longer memory than Moreva. It can have the argument.

q_knots_round_nothing_decide.speaker: Sauve Mor
q_knots_round_nothing_decide.text: Mor'oul. — My grandfather put the first eel back for them, he said, the ones under the water, so they would know. And they are sending the knots back. — What does that mean? You have been down there and I have only been over it a thousand times with a pole. Say what we do.

choices.text: Ring the Fog Bell for them until the ringer comes up.
Take the knots to Saeva. New lanterns, sent out properly.
Back in the traps. Let the water decide.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Sauve Mor
work_going.text: The water gives work to whoever asks it. I am asking it for you. Here.

greetings.text: Down. Lower. The watch looks at the boards, not under them. Follow me to the traps, and don't talk.
Fell-boots, in a marsh. Take them off or learn to walk in them. Down. Follow me to the traps.
A Vale walk. Heel first, like the ground owes you. Here it doesn't. Down. Follow me to the traps.
Ash-grey, and loud on boards. The fog will like you. The boards won't. Down. Follow me to the traps.
Wood-feet. You walk like the ground is roots. Here it's boards over water, and boards talk. Down. Follow me to the traps.
A Tollmere hand. Ink under the nails. You'll know his book better than he does, then. Down. Follow me to the traps.
Seen. She saw you, and now she's looking where you were. Back up to the landing's edge. Come again, lower, where she isn't.
His box is on the boards at the south-east edge. He sleeps with his mouth open. Don't wake it.
The sack. It won't see you. Neither will he, if you do it right.
There he goes. Round and round. Be where he isn't.
Quiet. Good. Give it here.
Look at him. Standing there like a man waiting to be told his own name.
You came back up. He didn't. My man in Gullhithe says the page is worth more now it's the only one.
Moreva rings the Fog Bell every quarter hour the fog is down, badly, turn about. On the ninth night somebody rang it back from under the water, once, in time. We have rung it better since.
Nine new lanterns went out on the south channel with the old knots, sung. The traps come up clean now. I miss the knots, which is a stupid thing to miss.
The knots came up again on Hushday, in the same traps, tied tighter. I put them back. The water can have the argument; I have the pole.

notes: The one voice of Saeva (sedgemire), written with the atlas: A lantern came back up the channel against the current, in a weave the lantern-makers stopped using eighty years ago.

greet.speaker: Lisse Tal
greet.text: Tal. Lisse. Sit on the boards, if you like; you are between the racks and the water, which is where everything here is.

hub.speaker: Lisse Tal
hub.text: Ask what you like. My hands will not stop, but my ears do.

choices.text: What came back up the channel?
How do you know a lantern's maker?
The lantern that came back up the channel.
It's your great-grandmother's weave, for a Gosford carter she named Ennet.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Lisse Tal
topic_1.text: A lantern. Out on the water they go down the south channel to the sea, and they come apart on the way, which is the burial; that is what a lantern is for. This one came back up, against the current, lit, and fetched up on our landing at dawn. — The weave is my great-grandmother's. We stopped weaving it eighty years ago. The strand of hair in it is grey. Somebody made a lantern in her way, with her hair, eighty years after she stopped, and sent it home.

topic_2.speaker: Lisse Tal
topic_2.text: The twist. Every family twists the rush a different way and every weaver a little differently inside that. A lantern is a letter. Most people only read the light. — The Order at Pilgrim's Ash buys our old weaves to hang in the chapter-bell. The knights say the lanterns and the bells are the same thing said twice, and I think they are right, and I think they are very far from the water to be right about it.

bye.speaker: Lisse Tal
bye.text: If you see a lantern on the water that is going the wrong way, do not follow it. Tell us.

q_against_the_current_offer.speaker: Lisse Tal
q_against_the_current_offer.text: Against the current, lit, and my great-grandmother's twist, and her hair in it. — A lantern is a letter. Most people only read the light. I have read this one forty times and it says one thing: somebody is still weaving her way, eighty years after she put down the rush. — Saoul, down the south channel, where the old village left its lanterns for Sa'oul. Somebody relights them every night. Go and see whose hands.

choices.text: I'll go down to Saoul.
Not now.

q_against_the_current_accept.speaker: Lisse Tal
q_against_the_current_accept.text: After dark the wisps come over the pool. They are what a burial becomes when nobody sings. — Sing, if you can. If you cannot, be quick.

q_against_the_current_decide_send_it_out.speaker: Lisse Tal
q_against_the_current_decide_send_it_out.text: Sung, all three voices, from the landing, tonight. If it comes back again, I will know she wants it home.

q_against_the_current_decide_hang_it_at_.speaker: Lisse Tal
q_against_the_current_decide_hang_it_at_.text: At the pool, then, on the last stilt, lit. — She is keeping them. I should help.

q_against_the_current_decide_sell_it_to_.speaker: Lisse Tal
q_against_the_current_decide_sell_it_to_.text: The knights say a lantern and a bell are the same thing said twice. — Let it be said the second way, then, in the grey. They pay in marks and they burn the lights on Candle Night. She would have liked Candle Night.

q_against_the_current_decide.speaker: Lisse Tal
q_against_the_current_decide.text: Ennet. — She named a drowned Vale man so he would not go out unsung, and wove his light, and went on weaving it somewhere where the current runs the other way. — That is a Tal. That is exactly a Tal. — The lantern is on my bench. It is lit. Tell me what I do with it.

choices.text: Send it out again, down the south channel, and sing it.
Hang it at Saoul with hers.
The Order would hang it in the chapter-bell.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Lisse Tal
work_going.text: I weave without talking. The work other people want, I will tell you out loud.

greetings.text: Sung, all three voices, and it went out on the south channel and did not come back. My mother says that means it got where it was going. My mother says a great many things.
Her lantern hangs on the last stilt at Saoul with the others, lit. I row out and trim them on Tolldays. There is one more every month. I do not know who is weaving them. I think I do.
They hung it in the chapter-bell at Pilgrim's Ash and lit it on Candle Night. A knight wrote to say the bell rings a little softer with it in. That is a Tal lantern for you.

notes: The one voice of Nauvissa (sedgemire), written with the atlas: The grey moves up the Greyreed a reed-bed a year; Nauvissa wants to know which of the four accounts is right before they decide whether to move.

greet.speaker: Ossa Lissa
greet.text: Lissa. Ossa. You have come from the ash side; you smell of it. Sit by the fire. It is grey reed. Listen.

hub.speaker: Ossa Lissa
hub.text: Ask.

choices.text: Why do the Order buy grey reeds?
The grey is moving up the Greyreed?
You want to know which account is right.
It comes in at night and goes back by day. The nets were torn from inside.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Ossa Lissa
topic_1.text: Wicks. A grey reed burns slow and even and makes a sound as it goes, a small voice, like somebody saying a word in the next room. The knights say it keeps them awake on the night watch. I think it keeps them company. — They pay in bread and salt and news of the Choir, and the news is better than the bread.

topic_2.speaker: Ossa Lissa
topic_2.text: A bed a year. When I was a girl the grey reeds were at the ash's edge, a mile south. Now they are at our landing. Next year they are under my floor. — The four accounts each tell me something different to do. The Bell says it does not matter. The Candle says talk more and stay. The Breath says go north. The Tide says wait, it goes out and comes back. I am reedfolk. I was raised on the Tide. I am waiting. I would like somebody to tell me whether waiting is still the same thing it was.

bye.speaker: Ossa Lissa
bye.text: Walk north, when you go. Not because the grey is south. Because the eels are north, and somebody should eat tonight.

q_which_account_offer.speaker: Ossa Lissa
q_which_account_offer.text: I want to know whether waiting is still the same thing it was. That is not the same question, and it is the only one that matters to a woman with a floor. — The watchman at the South Stilts says the grey comes in at night and goes back by day. Nobody believes him. I half believe him, which is the worst way to believe anything. Go and stand a night with him. If he is right, the Tide is right, and I can go on waiting with a clear mind.

choices.text: I'll stand a night at the stilts.
Not now.

q_which_account_accept.speaker: Ossa Lissa
q_which_account_accept.text: Take grey reed for your fire. It keeps a watcher company. The knights say so and they would know; they do nothing else.

q_which_account_decide_wait.speaker: Ossa Lissa
q_which_account_decide_wait.text: Then we wait. And we sing the round while we wait, all three voices, so that if it listens the way the water listens it will hear who is here.
