q_which_account_decide_go_north.speaker: Ossa Lissa
q_which_account_decide_go_north.text: North. — Ollo Nauve will build us a boat each and grumble about the price. We will take the grey reed with us. It is the only thing here that has never once complained.

q_which_account_decide_keep_the_watch.speaker: Ossa Lissa
q_which_account_decide_keep_the_watch.text: The Candle, then, from a reedfolk mouth. The knights will be astonished. — I will man the stilts myself the first night and tell the watchman he was right, and he will be unbearable.

q_which_account_decide.speaker: Ossa Lissa
q_which_account_decide.text: In and back. — Like water. — I was raised on the Tide. Everything goes out and comes back, the Tide says, the water and the dead and the names, and you wait, and waiting is a thing you do and not a thing you fail to do. — And now the grey does it too. So. Tell me. I will do what you say and blame you after, which is the reedfolk way.

choices.text: The Tide is right. Wait.
Go north to the Landing while it still goes back.
Stay, keep the stilts manned, and talk to the knights.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Ossa Lissa
work_going.text: There is always work. The Tide brings it in. This is what it brought this week.

greetings.text: We wait, and sing the round while we wait, all three voices. It came to the stilts at the new moon and went back before light. The round is getting better. So is it.
Half the houses are on Ollo's boats and half are still arguing on the stilts. The grey reed went first, on the lead boat. It did not complain.
The watchman is unbearable, as I said he would be. The knights buy our wicks and ask after him by name. The stilts are lit all night, and nothing has torn a net from inside since.

notes: The one voice of Oulea (sedgemire), written with the atlas: The tide came in over the shell bank for the first time in anyone's memory, and left something on the pans.

greet.speaker: Meo Sa
greet.text: Sa. Meo. You are standing on salt; everything here is. It gets into the boots and then into the bread and then into you. Welcome to Oulea.

hub.speaker: Meo Sa
hub.text: What is it?

choices.text: What did the tide leave on the pans?
Why did the Salt Isles ships stop?
The footprints on your pans.
They went down the harbour steps into the sea. The chart says a ship is due.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Meo Sa
topic_1.text: Footprints. On the new salt, in the morning, after a tide that came higher than the shell bank, which it has not done in the three hundred years my family has written tides on that post. — Bare feet. Coming up out of the sea and across the pans and back again. Small ones. The Tide account says the drowned will walk when the flood comes back. I have boiled salt my whole life on the Tide account. I would rather it had waited until I was dead.

topic_2.speaker: Meo Sa
topic_2.text: Nobody knows. Forty years ago the last of them came in at midsummer and traded as always and sailed, and the next midsummer nobody came, and nobody since. We put up one tent for them at the Traders' Post every longest day anyway. — My father said they found a better salt. My mother said they found out something about us. I do not know which is worse.

bye.speaker: Meo Sa
bye.text: Go inland before the evening tide. Not because it is dangerous. Because I would like to be the only one watching it.

q_what_the_tide_left_offer.speaker: Meo Sa
q_what_the_tide_left_offer.text: Small ones. Bare. Up out of the sea and across and back, on salt that was not there the day before. — I have written a tide on that post every day for forty years and my mother before me and her mother before her, and this spring the tide came over the bank, and I wrote it, and then I did not know what to write under it. — There are more prints up at the Salt Pans, the rakers say, going the other way. Go and see which way.

choices.text: I'll walk up to the Salt Pans.
Not now.

q_what_the_tide_left_accept.speaker: Meo Sa
q_what_the_tide_left_accept.text: Walk on the crust, not the brine. And if you see a child on the flats, do not call out to it. — I do not know why I said that. Go on.

q_what_the_tide_left_decide_put_up_the_t.speaker: Meo Sa
q_what_the_tide_left_decide_put_up_the_t.text: All year. — My father said they found a better salt. My mother said they found out something about us. I will set out the best we boil, and we shall see which.

q_what_the_tide_left_decide_write_it_tru.speaker: Meo Sa
q_what_the_tide_left_decide_write_it_tru.text: As it came: the height, and the prints, and the word due. The post will be the first thing on this coast that tells the truth about this year. It may be the last.

q_what_the_tide_left_decide_to_the_spire.speaker: Meo Sa
q_what_the_tide_left_decide_to_the_spire.text: The Spire, then. They will argue about the word for a year and publish nothing. That will give the ship time.

q_what_the_tide_left_decide.speaker: Meo Sa
q_what_the_tide_left_decide.text: Due. — Forty years since a Salt Isles sail, and the Builders' bells ringing for one that has not set out, and children's feet on my salt going inland and coming back. — The Tide says what goes out comes back. It does not say what it will be. — What do I write? Say.

choices.text: Put up the tent all year. Set out salt.
Write it on the post as it came.
Send the chart to the Circle.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Meo Sa
work_going.text: Salt does not boil itself, and neither does anything else on this coast. This is what is wanted, and what it pays.

greetings.text: The traders' tent is up all year with our best salt in it. The gulls have had some. Nothing has come off the sea for it yet. It is due.
The post says this year as it came: the height, the prints, and due. Children walk over from the Salt Pans to read it. They read it to each other in whispers, which is the right way.
The Circle has written twice to ask what the word means and whether I am sure it is a word. I have written back once: it is due. We are keeping each other busy.

notes: The one voice of Elderhold (briarwold), written with the atlas: The elder doorposts have flowered out of season, and the lodge wants the Standing Moot's opinion without going to ask for it.

greet.speaker: Wenna Holt
greet.text: Holt. Wenna. You are at the Wold's door; you may stand at it. Whether you go through it is another matter, and not mine alone.

hub.speaker: Wenna Holt
hub.text: Ask, and I may answer.

choices.text: Why are the doorposts growing?
Which trees go down to the Mere?
Is it true the Woodfolk have no law?
A Tollmere bookbinder sends the Builders' words from your quarry.
The doorposts flowered in the frost.
Forty trees that hadn't asked. Poachers, a saw, and your mark.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Wenna Holt
topic_1.text: They are elder. Elder does not know it has been made into a door; it simply goes on being elder, and we let it, and every year the lodge is a little taller at the door than at the back. — This spring they flowered in the frost. Elder does not flower in the frost. I have written to the Standing Moot's keepers, which is to say I have oiled a stone and said so aloud, and I am waiting. The Wold is slow to answer. It is not slow to notice.

topic_2.speaker: Wenna Holt
topic_2.text: The ones that have finished. You can tell a tree that has finished; it stands differently. The Tallymen would like us to tell them by the girth, and pay by the girth, and we tell them by the standing, and they pay what they are told. — Every tree that goes down the Wold Water is one that asked. That is the whole of the custom, and the whole of the argument, and the Circle has written three pamphlets about it.

topic_3.speaker: Wenna Holt
topic_3.text: We have custom and bows. Custom says you do not take more than you need. The bows are for the ones who do not listen to custom. Tollmere says that is not law. Tollmere has a building full of law and a room under it full of thieves, and we have neither, so.

bye.speaker: Wenna Holt
bye.text: Go gently in the Wold. Nothing will stop you. That is not the same as being welcome.

q_the_stride_dedication_to_elderhold.speaker: Wenna Holt
q_the_stride_dedication_to_elderhold.text: From the Old Quarry. — The block that would not come out. We left it hanging because it asked to be left, the way a tree asks. — Walk it anyway, it says. Yes. That is the Wold's custom too, and the Builders knew it, and Tollmere laid their road and forgot. — I will oil the block. Tell the binder the third line means what it says, and that she should stop putting question marks after it.

q_flowered_in_the_frost_offer.speaker: Wenna Holt
q_flowered_in_the_frost_offer.text: They did. I oiled a stone and said so, aloud, which is how you tell the Moot a thing, and I am waiting. The Wold is slow to answer. It is not slow to notice. — You are not Woodfolk. You may go and listen where we would not. Climb the Grey Man. The hum comes across the Greatwood to the top of it, and the foresters say there is a word in it this spring, and they will not say what, because saying it would be asking.

choices.text: I'll climb the Grey Man.
Not now.

q_flowered_in_the_frost_accept.speaker: Wenna Holt
q_flowered_in_the_frost_accept.text: Do not say the word back. Listen, and then come down, and then go where it sends you. It will send you somewhere. It always does.

q_flowered_in_the_frost_decide_plant_for.speaker: Wenna Holt
q_flowered_in_the_frost_decide_plant_for.text: Forty, with the whole lodge, this autumn, and I will cut the notches off myself with the same knife. The ledger will be right. The trees will not be the same trees. Nothing ever is.

q_flowered_in_the_frost_decide_slowly.speaker: Wenna Holt
q_flowered_in_the_frost_decide_slowly.text: No rope, no bark, no leave, and nobody will say why. It is slow. It is the slowest thing in the world. It works.

q_flowered_in_the_frost_decide_make_them.speaker: Wenna Holt
q_flowered_in_the_frost_decide_make_them.text: The Guild's price. — Tollmere pays for what it is told, by the girth. I will take their marks and buy forty saplings from the Vale, and the Vale will charge me, and that is three wrongs, and the trees will grow anyway.

q_flowered_in_the_frost_decide.speaker: Wenna Holt
q_flowered_in_the_frost_decide.text: Forty that had not finished, with my mark cut on them by a saw. — The elder knew before I did. — Custom says you do not take more than you need, and the bows are for the ones who do not listen, and the bows have been used. Now the custom. You are standing at the Wold's door. Say what goes through it.

choices.text: Plant forty. Cut forty notches off.
The Wold's way. No rope, and nothing said.
Take the Guild's price and plant with it.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Wenna Holt
work_going.text: The Wold asks, and you answer or you do not. This is what it is asking this week.

greetings.text: Forty in the ground and forty notches off. You may go through the door, if you like. Mind the flowers. There are none. Mind them anyway.
The rafters could not buy rope in the Wold this autumn, or bark, or leave to cross. Nobody told them why. They go down to the Vale for rope now and pay twice for it. It is slow. It works.
Forty Vale saplings in the ground, bought with Guild marks, and the Vale charged me for the carting. Three wrongs. The saplings do not know. One of them has already asked for more light.

notes: The one voice of Rookhold (briarwold), written with the atlas: The Old Gate's doors were found open at dawn, from the far side.

greet.speaker: Edda Thornby
greet.text: Thornby. Edda. Keeper. The gate behind me is the Old Gate, and it is shut, and it is going to stay shut while I am standing here, which is a long time yet.

hub.speaker: Edda Thornby
hub.text: Say what you need to say. Quietly. The thorn listens.

choices.text: Why does only the Old Gate still close?
What happened at dawn?
Is the Briar keeping something out or in?
You want someone to look at the far side of the gate.
The patch that moved is standing at your gate, on the far side.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Edda Thornby
topic_1.text: Because we keep it. There were four gates and four lodges, once. The northern gate's keepers went up to Harrow Tor to clear the road in the Chain Years and did not come down, and the Moot and south gates' keepers went to the Vale when the carts stopped. We stayed. — A gate is a promise that something will be let through and something will not. A promise nobody sleeps against is a hole.

topic_2.speaker: Edda Thornby
topic_2.text: The doors were open. Not broken: open, and the bar lifted from the far side and laid on the ground on our side, neatly, as if somebody had been let in and was polite about it. The youngest was asleep against them, as she should have been, and she woke up on the other side of the gate. She came back through and closed it and has not spoken since. — I would like somebody to go and look at the far side. Not through. Look.

topic_3.speaker: Edda Thornby
topic_3.text: I have read both pamphlets. Alder Wyke is a friend and the Circle is not, and I still do not know. I know this: the thorn is thickest on our side because we lay it. Whatever the Builders meant, it is our laying that stands now. What it keeps is whatever we are keeping.

bye.speaker: Edda Thornby
bye.text: When you go, go west. Not because east is closed. Because I asked.

q_opened_from_the_far_side_offer.speaker: Edda Thornby
q_opened_from_the_far_side_offer.text: Look. Not go through. — The doors were open at dawn, the bar lifted from the far side and laid on our side as neat as a folded shirt, and the youngest asleep on the other side of them, as she should have been, only on the wrong side. She came back and shut it and has not spoken since. — Go to the Gate Stone. Things come to it at night now. Then go somewhere high and look over.

choices.text: I'll look. Not through.
Not now.

q_opened_from_the_far_side_accept.speaker: Edda Thornby
q_opened_from_the_far_side_accept.text: Good. — The verderer's tower is the only high place on the east. He will not come down. Go up to him.

q_opened_from_the_far_side_decide_sleep_.speaker: Edda Thornby
q_opened_from_the_far_side_decide_sleep_.text: Facing the Wold, as it was kept. The youngest can sit up with me and learn it again. She swore the wrong way round. It is not her fault. Nobody told her which way the promise faces.

q_opened_from_the_far_side_decide_leave_.speaker: Edda Thornby
q_opened_from_the_far_side_decide_leave_.text: From both sides. — That is not a Rookhold answer. I do not know what kind of answer it is. I will leave the bar where it was laid and sleep next to it, and we shall see who picks it up.

q_opened_from_the_far_side_decide_tell_f.speaker: Edda Thornby
q_opened_from_the_far_side_decide_tell_f.text: Alder. — He counts the patches and walks the Briar every morning and his count is going up. He should know one of them is at my door. I will send the youngest; it will make her speak.

q_opened_from_the_far_side_decide.speaker: Edda Thornby
q_opened_from_the_far_side_decide.text: The size of a door. — At my gate. — Something let itself in to look at us and was polite about it, and left the bar on our side so we would know, and now it is standing on the other side of the thorn where the patch used to be. — I have read both pamphlets and I still do not know what the Briar keeps. I know what I keep. Tell me how.

choices.text: Sleep against it yourself, facing the Wold.
Leave the bar lying. Keep the promise from both sides.
Send word to Alder Wyke.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Edda Thornby
work_going.text: The thorn keeps us busy. What it does not keep us busy with, you may have.

greetings.text: The youngest sits up with me now, facing the Wold, and she swears it the right way round. Nothing has stood on the far side of the thorn since. I sleep better on the ground than I ever did in a bed.
The bar has not moved. Some nights something on the far side of the thorn sleeps against it too. I can hear it breathe. We keep the promise together, it and I, and neither of us says so.
Alder Wyke came up the thorn himself and counted the patch at my gate and wrote it in his book. The youngest carried the word, and she has not stopped talking since. I asked for that.

notes: The one voice of Hazelwick (briarwold), written with the atlas: One of the stools has not grown back after cutting, the first in seven hundred years, and the family it belongs to wants it named before the Roll takes theirs.

greet.speaker: Aggie Coppice
greet.text: Coppice. Aggie. Reeve. If you are here to buy rods the price is the price and I will tell you what I think of it, and if you are here for anything else I will tell you what I think of that too.

hub.speaker: Aggie Coppice
hub.text: Go on. The stools can wait; they are very old.

choices.text: What is the round?
Which stool has not grown back?
Tam Withy asks why the Wold has stopped selling him rods.
The Fennick stool hasn't grown back.
The stool went into its rods. And a Fennick's moss was let go.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Aggie Coppice
topic_1.text: Seven years. Every stool in Hazelwick is cut to the ground once in seven, and grows back seven years of rods, straight as a Sayer's excuses. The book says which family cuts which stool which year. It has said it for seven hundred years and been argued with for all of them. — Tam Withy at Hazelcombe weaves the rods into hurdles and pays me what he pays. I tell him it is an insult. He agrees. We have been having that conversation for twenty years and it is the best part of both our summers.

topic_2.speaker: Aggie Coppice
topic_2.text: The Fennick stool. Cut last winter, as the book said, and it has put up nothing. Not a shoot. Seven hundred years it has come back, and the Fennicks cut it every seventh, and this year it is a stump and a stump only. — The Fennicks are a Vale family and have been in the book since before there was a Vale. Old Aud Fennick walked south this spring, I hear. I have not said so to the stool.

bye.speaker: Aggie Coppice
bye.text: Mind the stools as you go. They look like stumps. They are not stumps. They are only resting.

q_pens_with_no_gate_the_rods.speaker: Aggie Coppice
q_pens_with_no_gate_the_rods.text: Because he asked for rods for pens. — The Wold does not sell hazel for a pen nothing can walk out of. A thing that has gone grey is let go, here, the way we let a named moss go when there is nobody left to say it. Tell Tam he can have all the rods he likes for a fold. For a pen with no gate he can cut his own, and his hands will know what they are doing even if he does not.

q_the_fennick_stool_offer.speaker: Aggie Coppice
q_the_fennick_stool_offer.text: Not a shoot. Seven hundred years it has come back and this year it is a stump. — The Fennicks are Vale folk and have cut that stool every seventh since before there was a Vale to be from, and the last of them has walked south, and I have not told the stool, because I am a sensible woman and it is a stump. — The last rods off it are drying at the Rod Stacks. If there is anything left of the Fennicks in this wood it is in those. Go and look at them. You will know them; I chalked the tie.

choices.text: I'll look at the rods.
Not now.

q_the_fennick_stool_accept.speaker: Aggie Coppice
q_the_fennick_stool_accept.text: And if Tam Withy's cutters are at the Stacks, tell them the price is the price. They will not believe you either.

q_the_fennick_stool_decide_keep_the_name.speaker: Aggie Coppice
q_the_fennick_stool_decide_keep_the_name.text: The Fennick stool, in the book, every seventh year, cut or not, as long as I am reading it and after. Somebody will argue. I will read it aloud to them.

q_the_fennick_stool_decide_plant_the_rod.speaker: Aggie Coppice
q_the_fennick_stool_decide_plant_the_rod.text: Sets round the stump, as thick as a thumb, with their roots out already. — In seven years there will be a stool, and it will be the Fennick stool, and it will not be, and the book will say Fennick and I will not explain.

q_the_fennick_stool_decide_let_it_go.speaker: Aggie Coppice
q_the_fennick_stool_decide_let_it_go.text: Let go, then. The Holts will take it. Wil married one; that is near enough to a Fennick for a wood. — The book will say Holt. I will read it aloud slowly, the first time.

q_the_fennick_stool_decide.speaker: Aggie Coppice
q_the_fennick_stool_decide.text: Wil Fennick. — I knew him. I was a girl. He married a Holt and sat on the bench outside Elderhold and told the whole Wold that hazel was only a tree with good manners. — They let his moss go the week she went. And the stool put its last seven years into the rods and lay down. — The book is mine. What does it say?

choices.text: The Fennick stool. As long as there is a book.
Plant the rooted rods round the stump.
Let it go, like a moss. Give it to a Wold family.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Aggie Coppice
work_going.text: Work. Here is what the Wold wants done this week, and none of it is hazel.

greetings.text: The book says the Fennick stool this year, cut or not. A Holt argued at the reading. I read it aloud to him twice. He has not argued since.
The sets round the old stump have all leafed, thick as a thumb. In seven years it will be the Fennick stool. I will not explain.
The Holts cut their first rods off the old Fennick stool at the turn of the year. The book says Holt now. I read it out slowly the first time. The second time came easier.

notes: The one voice of Ormhold (briarwold), written with the atlas: The Listeners left a trunk at Ormhold in 1038 and never came back for it; it has started to smell of the sea.

greet.speaker: Nessa Ashby
greet.text: Ashby. Nessa. Ormhold. There are beds, if you are the Circle, at the Circle's rate; if you are not, there is floor, at mine.

hub.speaker: Nessa Ashby
hub.text: What do you want in the Northwold?

choices.text: You guided the Listeners through the northern gate?
Why charge the Circle for the beds?
The Listeners' trunk smells of the sea.
There's sea-sand on the gate step. Something's clearing the road for them.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Nessa Ashby
topic_1.text: To it. Not through. The Wold does not go through; that is the custom. Two Listeners and a chart-maker, in 1038, with a great deal of paper. I waited three days at the gate stone. They came back on the fourth from the far side, with salt in their boots and the chart-maker not speaking, and slept here one more night, and went home, and wrote their report, which nobody reads. — They left a trunk. I have not opened it. This spring it smells of the sea, and there is no sea north of here.

topic_2.speaker: Nessa Ashby
topic_2.text: Because they used them. And because while they owe me they write to me, and while they write to me somebody in the Spire has to remember there is a gate in the north of the Wold that their people went through and came back from. — I have never opened a reply. I know what they say. Paying would end it.

bye.speaker: Nessa Ashby
bye.text: The north path is clear to the tor. Past the tor, keep to the stones.

q_the_listeners_trunk_offer.speaker: Nessa Ashby
q_the_listeners_trunk_offer.text: It does, and there is no sea north of here, and I have not opened it, because the Wold does not open what it is given to keep. — They came back from the far side on the fourth day with salt in their boots and wrote their report, which nobody reads. — The foresters say the road to the northern gate is clear every morning. The gate's keepers carried every stone they cleared up Harrow Tor, in the Chain Years, and did not come down. Go up the tor. Look at the road from the top, where they looked.

choices.text: I'll climb Harrow Tor.
Not now.

q_the_listeners_trunk_accept.speaker: Nessa Ashby
q_the_listeners_trunk_accept.text: Look. Do not go through. — That is not a warning. It is the custom. The warning is that the road is clear.

q_the_listeners_trunk_decide_open_it.speaker: Nessa Ashby
q_the_listeners_trunk_decide_open_it.text: ...A notebook, in sealskin, and sand. Take the book; you opened it, it is yours to read. I will put the sand on the fire. I do not want to know what it smells like when it burns.

q_the_listeners_trunk_decide_send_it_to_.speaker: Nessa Ashby
q_the_listeners_trunk_decide_send_it_to_.text: Unopened, with the bill, and a note to say it smells of the sea. They will not read the note. They will pay the bill. That is how it has always gone.

q_the_listeners_trunk_decide_leave_it_at.speaker: Nessa Ashby
q_the_listeners_trunk_decide_leave_it_at.text: On the step, for whoever clears the road. — Yes. The Wold does not go through. It can leave things at the door.

q_the_listeners_trunk_decide.speaker: Nessa Ashby
q_the_listeners_trunk_decide.text: For them. — Clearing the road back. After five years. — I have kept that trunk under a blanket in the back room for five years and dusted it on Kindledays and not once asked it anything. You have been to the stone. Say what I do with it.

choices.text: Open it.
Send it to the Spire, unopened, with the bill.
Leave it on the step at the gate.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Nessa Ashby
work_going.text: The lodge has work it cannot do itself. Here is the list, and here is what it pays, which is less than it should.

greetings.text: I put the sand on the fire. It smelled of a harbour I have never seen. I have not been able to get it out of the back room. I have stopped trying.
The Spire paid the bill and did not read the note. Something came up the road to the gate in the night last week and stood at the step, and found nothing on it, and went back.
The trunk was gone from the step in the morning, the road was swept clean to the Stone, and there was a handful of sea-sand where the trunk had stood. I have left the sand.

notes: The one voice of Ruddow (skerrow), written with the atlas: Rudd have finally asked for the forty head, through the player as Kharrow's go-between, and the reason is on the roll of their dead.

greet.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
greet.text: Ushra ko-Rudd. I keep the memory of this clan, and the account, which is the same thing said with numbers. You are standing in Ruddow; the wall behind you was a giant's back.

hub.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
hub.text: Speak.

choices.text: What does Kharrow owe Rudd?
Why ask for it now?
What is the wall made of?
There is a Builders' channel behind the Rust Scar, and it is wet.
Rudd are asking for the forty head at last.
Torkh laid the coin himself, at night, to keep it out of the song.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
topic_1.text: Forty head and a hearth. The winter of the long snow, when the Windgate came down and Kharrow's herds were buried in the gorge, Rudd fed Kharrow from our own fold and gave a hearth to a family whose house was under the snow. Forty head. We have been asked three times to take payment and three times we have said it is forgiven. — It is not forgiven until it is paid. That is the whole of the Rope-Song in one line. A debt is a rope between two clans. Pay it and the rope goes slack.

topic_2.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
topic_2.text: Because the Toll hums and the clans are counting what holds them together, and Rudd has counted, and the rope to Kharrow is the one we would keep. — If Kharrow pays, it is only forty head. If Kharrow refuses, it is a quarrel, and a quarrel is a rope too. Either is better than a debt nobody has spoken of in a hundred years. I am the one who speaks of it. I would like it heard.

topic_3.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
topic_3.text: A giant's back. Each vertebra a clan-cairn's worth of bone. Rudd found it in the scree above the dale when the Oskeld glacier went back, and carried it down one bone at a time, and it took nine winters. The Sayers say it is the same giant as the Rib Cathedral's. Rudd say it is ours.

bye.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
bye.text: Go with the rope, as we say. Mind which end you are holding.

q_the_third_arch_ruddows_water.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
q_the_third_arch_ruddows_water.text: Wet. — One day this spring the Scar ran clear, and every Rudd child born that day has the Scar's name, and the next morning it ran red again, as it always has. We said the fell stopped bleeding for a day. I wrote it in the account as a day owed to nobody. — If the clear water went into the Builders' stone, it went somewhere. Follow it down, and tell whoever is drinking it that Rudd would like to know.

q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_offer.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_offer.text: Through you, if you will carry it. Kharrow will not hear it from a Rudd; they will hear it from a go-between, because then it is a matter and not a quarrel. — The reason is on our roll of the dead. I will not tell you which line. Go up the chain and speak to our fosterling first. He is nine and wears a man's token and he knows more about it than Kharrow does, because nobody has told him not to.

choices.text: I'll carry it up the chain.
Not now.

q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_accept.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_accept.text: Wall on your right on the stair. Everyone who went over the edge went over on the left.

q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_decide_take_th.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_decide_take_th.text: Paid. I will write it paid, and the rope goes slack, and nobody sings it, and I will know. That is what a memory-keeper is for: to know the things that are not sung.

q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_decide_ask_in_.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_decide_ask_in_.text: In the hall, before the seven, with the bone passed hand to hand. Torkh will say the price aloud, because he must, and the song will be a line longer. It is a quarrel. A quarrel is a rope too.

q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_decide_bring_k.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_decide_bring_k.text: The boy. — We sent him up to say forgiven with his feet. Kharrow kept him, because a debt is not forgiven until it is paid. — Then let this be the payment: he comes home. I will go up the chain for him myself.

q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_decide.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
q_forty_head_and_a_hearth_decide.text: In the dark. Twice. — So that Kharrow's verse would not have to say that Rudd died for Kharrow's herd. — A debt paid in the dark is a rope cut in the dark. — It is Rudd's account. I keep it. Tell me what goes in it.

choices.text: Take the coin. It is paid.
Ask for the forty head in the hall, and have it sung.
Ask for the boy.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Ushra ko-Rudd
work_going.text: Rudd keep an account of what is owed and of what wants doing. This is the second.

greetings.text: Written paid. The rope is slack and nobody sings it, and I know. A memory-keeper sleeps on what she knows. I sleep well enough.
Torkh said the price aloud in the hall, with the bone passed hand to hand, and the song is a line longer. We quarrel over it at every Moot now. A quarrel is a rope too. It holds.
Kharrow have agreed. Kun comes down the chain at the thaw, and he will be wearing a Kharrow cloak, and he will sing me their verse, and I will let him. A debt is paid. A boy is a boy.

notes: The one voice of Ghastfell (skerrow), written with the atlas: Ghast want the bridge mended and the song of forgiveness stopped; Kharrow want neither.

greet.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
greet.text: Ko-Ghast, Dagga. Ladder-warden. You came up the long ladders; well done. Most outlanders look down on the fourth.

hub.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
hub.text: What do you want, outlander?

choices.text: Why has Ghast never mended the bridge?
Would you mend it, if you could?
What is at the bottom of the gorge?
Ghast want the bridge mended. I could carry that to Kharrow.
Kharrow says the bridge is yours to mend.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
topic_1.text: Because the Moot forgave us, and sings that it forgave us every morning, in Kharrow's hall, before food. A forgiveness sung every morning is a debt with a nicer voice. — We cut Kharrow's chain in the year of the broken bridge. There was blood. The Moot forgave. And if we mend the bridge the song stops, and if the song stops the forgiveness is forgotten, and a forgotten forgiveness goes back to being a debt. So we climb. It is a very long way to keep a grudge polished.

topic_2.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
topic_2.text: Tomorrow. I would mend it tomorrow and cross it drunk. — But the elders say the song is what holds Ghast in the Rope-Song at all, the forgiveness verse, and a clan with no verse is a clan the Breath takes. Ghorr had no verse. You have heard of Ghorr. Nobody has.

topic_3.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
topic_3.text: The chain we cut, still hanging, and the bridge's anchor on the far side with a mark on it that is no clan's. The goats cross by the chain. Goats do not know about the Moot.

bye.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
bye.text: Down the ladders face in. Always face in. The mountain likes to be looked at.

q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_offer.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_offer.text: You could. Everybody could. Nobody does. — A forgiveness sung every morning is a debt with a nicer voice. — Go down to the bridge first. The chain we cut is still hanging and the goats cross by it, and on the far anchor there is a mark that is no clan's, and I have looked at it through a glass every spring of my life and never been over to touch it. Wolves den under the stones. Take a spear. Take two.

choices.text: I'll go down to the bridge.
Not now.

q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_accept.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_accept.text: And if you cross by the chain, do not look down. The goats do not. That is the whole of their wisdom and it has kept them alive two hundred years.

q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_decide_mend_.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_decide_mend_.text: Mend it. — I will cut the first new link myself, and Kharrow will hear the hammer from their hall, and the song will stop or it will not, and either way I will cross drunk.

q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_decide_keep_.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_decide_keep_.text: In the song. — Yes. It is a very long way to keep a grudge polished, and it keeps Ghast in the Rope-Song, and I will keep the ladders oiled. Somebody has to be the one who climbs.

q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_decide_sing_.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_decide_sing_.text: Across the gorge. — Kharrow singing forgiveness at Ghast's own door, where we can hear it. They will say no. Ask anyway. If they say yes, I will not know what to do with my face.

q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_decide.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
q_a_debt_with_a_nicer_voice_decide.text: Mine to mend and theirs to sing. — And somebody setting stones on the Red Moor for a bridge, with our mark and theirs and a ring with a gap. — I am tired of this grudge. I have polished it my whole life and I would like to put it down. The ladders are mine. Say what Ghast does.

choices.text: Mend it.
Keep climbing. You're in the song.
Ask Kharrow to sing it here, once, across the gorge.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Dagga ko-Ghast
work_going.text: Ghast always have work. You have to climb up to it. Here.

greetings.text: The bridge is mended and I crossed it drunk, as I said I would. Kharrow still sing the forgiveness every morning. It holds without the ladders. I have nothing left to polish.
I oil the ladders every Skerrday and climb them every morning, and Kharrow sing us across. It is a long way to keep a grudge. My arms are the best in Ghast.
Kharrow came to the lip of the gorge at dawn and sang it once, across, at our door. I did not know what to do with my face. I have been told it was smiling.

notes: The one voice of Dreughow (skerrow), written with the atlas: Someone has painted an eighth verse on a Dreughow door overnight, in no clan's hand.

greet.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
greet.text: Ko-Dreugh, Brann. Mind the doors, the paint is wet on the third. It is always wet on one of them. That is the point.

hub.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
hub.text: Ask, and I will paint while you do.

choices.text: Why paint the verse on the doors?
What was painted on the door overnight?
Who was the first Brann?
The eighth verse on your ninth door.
The same verse is over Ghorrow's open door. In your blue.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
topic_1.text: Dreugh sing first at the Moot. Seven clans, seven verses, and ours opens the rope. If a stranger knocks on a Dreugh door he should know where he is in the song before he is let in. — I paint a word a day. By midwinter the verse is new again. My grandfather said a verse painted once is a sign and a verse painted every day is a prayer, and I do not know whether he was pious or just liked painting.

topic_2.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
topic_2.text: An eighth verse. On the ninth door, over our first, in a hand no clan uses. It is a verse's length and a verse's metre, and the words are Skerrish, and they do not mean anything, or they mean something nobody has said in a thousand years. — Four beats of silence every morning at Kharrow for the missing clan. Somebody has filled them in with paint. I have not painted over it. I cannot bring myself to. I have not read it aloud either.

topic_3.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
topic_3.text: The clan-books say he hung the first chain at Windgate and would not be roped while he did it. Kharrow's books say that was their Brann. We do not discuss it at the Moot.

bye.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
bye.text: Knock on any door on your way. Read it first.

q_the_ninth_door_offer.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
q_the_ninth_door_offer.text: Over our first, in a hand no clan uses, in my paint. — I have not painted over it. I cannot bring myself to. I have not read it aloud either. I stand in front of it every morning with the brush and then I go and paint the tenth door. — Somebody ground my blue and climbed my ladder and knew the metre. On Brindle Edge the children's ropes hang on the cairn; the Brindles say a rope has gone up this spring that no family owns. Go and look at the knots. Knots are a hand too.

choices.text: I'll look at the rope on the cairn.
Not now.

q_the_ninth_door_accept.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
q_the_ninth_door_accept.text: Mind the third door, the paint is wet. It is always wet on one of them. That is the point.

q_the_ninth_door_decide_paint_it_over.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
q_the_ninth_door_decide_paint_it_over.text: Over it, a word a day, the way I always do, and by midwinter the first verse will be new again and the eighth will be under it, the way the breath is under the song.

q_the_ninth_door_decide_leave_both.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
q_the_ninth_door_decide_leave_both.text: Both, then, one on the other. — A stranger knocking at the ninth door will not know where he is in the song. Nor do I. We can be lost together.

q_the_ninth_door_decide_to_the_memory_ke.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
q_the_ninth_door_decide_to_the_memory_ke.text: Dunna. — She keeps what Kharrow remembers, and the silence is after Kharrow's verse. I will copy it word by word on a board and send the board. I will not read it on the way.

q_the_ninth_door_decide.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
q_the_ninth_door_decide.text: Over Ghorrow's door, where no clan's mark is. — Painted by somebody who has watched a verse painted every day for a very long time and never been taught. — Four beats of silence every morning, and somebody has been listening to the silence. — The ninth door is mine to paint. Say what goes on it.

choices.text: Paint the first verse back over it.
Leave both.
Copy it for Dunna ko-Kharrow.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Brann ko-Dreugh
work_going.text: Dreugh want things done that are not painting. Here they are.

greetings.text: A word a day, and the first verse is new on the ninth door again, with the eighth under it the way the breath is under the song. Some mornings the blue has been touched before I come. I paint anyway.
Both verses, one on the other. A trader knocked at the ninth door and asked where he was in the song. I said I did not know either. He stayed for supper.
Dunna sent the board back with one word painted under the last line, in Kharrow's red: listened. I have hung it inside the ninth door, facing in.

notes: The one voice of Skarlow (skerrow), written with the atlas: Skarl's herders have seen a line of lights moving north along the Briar, beyond the wall, where there is no road.

greet.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
greet.text: Ko-Skarl. Varra. You came from the west; everybody does. Sit on the east side of the fire. We keep the west side for the wind.

hub.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
hub.text: Say it.

choices.text: Why do all the doors face east?
What are the lights?
The lights along the Briar.
The Watcher's turned to watch them go past. They're going out, not in.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
topic_1.text: The Skarl verse says the giants went east when they were breathed in, along a road on the far side of the thorn, and that they will come back along it. We would like to see them coming. — It is not hope. Skarl are not hopeful people. It is manners. If somebody has been gone a thousand years you should at least be facing the door.

topic_2.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
topic_2.text: A line of them. Moving north along the far side of the Briar, beyond the wall, slow, on three nights this spring. There is no road there that the Woodfolk know of, and the Woodfolk know every road there is and several there are not. — Nine lights. The same nine each time, the same spacing. I counted. Skarl count; it is the one thing we are known for, apart from the doors.

bye.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
bye.text: Go west when you go. You will anyway. Everybody does.

q_nine_lights_offer.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
q_nine_lights_offer.text: Nine. Same spacing, same pace, north, on three nights. — There is no road on that side of the thorn that the Woodfolk know of, and the Woodfolk know every road there is and several there are not. — Skarl are not hopeful people. We are counting people. I have counted them and I would like somebody to go and look at what I counted. Go up to the shieling first. The herders will not come down to tell me things; I have to send outlanders up.

choices.text: I'll go up to the shieling.
Not now.

q_nine_lights_accept.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
q_nine_lights_accept.text: Sit on the east side of their fire. They keep the west side for the wind, as we do. They will think better of you.

q_nine_lights_decide_rebuild_the_wall.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
q_nine_lights_decide_rebuild_the_wall.text: Stronger, and from our side, and we tell the Woodfolk it was pushed from ours. Honesty with a wall is the only kind that holds.

q_nine_lights_decide_face_east.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
q_nine_lights_decide_face_east.text: Count them. — That is what we do. Every night they come I will sit on the east side of the fire and count, and chalk it, and if one night it is eight, I will know somebody has stopped.

q_nine_lights_decide_tell_rookhold.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
q_nine_lights_decide_tell_rookhold.text: Edda. The Old Gate. — Her doors opened from the far side and my wall was pushed from this one. The thorn is having a busy spring. I will send the fastest herder down the thorn, and tell her to go round the Briar's End and not through it.

q_nine_lights_decide.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
q_nine_lights_decide.text: Out. — A thousand years of Skarl doors facing east for something to come back, and it is going the other way. — The Watcher turned his head to see them off. — Well. I am the herd-mother. I keep the cattle and the watch. Tell me what the watch does now.

choices.text: Rebuild the wall.
Face east and count them.
Send word to Edda Thornby at Rookhold.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Varra ko-Skarl
work_going.text: The herd wants what the herd wants. This is what the rest of us want.

greetings.text: The bone wall is up again, stronger, and the Woodfolk have been told it was pushed from our side. They thanked us for the honesty. The lights go past it at night, the other way.
Nine, every night they come, chalked on the east post. Last Hushday it was nine and something that was not quite a tenth. I did not chalk it. I watched it.
Edda Thornby sent my herder back with a strip of thorn bark, knotted twice. It means we keep the same promise from different doors. I have hung it on the Watcher.

notes: The one voice of Oskelcrag (skerrow), written with the atlas: An Oskel child walked up the mine road in her sleep and came back humming.

greet.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
greet.text: Ko-Oskel. Ebba. Lead-captain. You are standing on spoil; the whole village is. Oskel built on what came out of the mountain. It seemed polite.

hub.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
hub.text: Well, outlander?

choices.text: Why does nobody go up the Oskeld road?
What happened to the child?
Aske walked up the Oskeld road in her sleep.
The thralls in the rake hum it while they work. And the fire stops it.
Is there any work going?
I'll be on my way.

topic_1.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
topic_1.text: Because we sealed it. Oskel followed the silver into the mountain and the silver ran into bone, and the bone started to sing, and one day what was singing came up the shaft, and we sealed the shaft behind it and the road behind that. — Now we dig lead in the lower dale and we do not look up the road. I knock on the marker stone every morning so it knows we are still here and still not coming.

topic_2.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
topic_2.text: Aske. Nine. Walked up the Oskeld road in her sleep in the small hours, past the marker, past the shieling, to the sealed shaft, and sat down there, and was found at dawn humming a tune nobody in Oskelcrag knows. She is well. She eats. She hums it when she is not thinking. — The clan-books say the thing in the shaft is holding a note. I would very much like to know whose, and I would very much like it not to be teaching it to children.

bye.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
bye.text: If you go up the road, and you should not, knock on the stone first. Twice. So it knows it is you.

q_askes_tune_offer.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
q_askes_tune_offer.text: To the shaft, and sat down, and was found humming. She is well. She eats. She hums it when she is not thinking. — I would like to know whose tune it is, and I cannot go up the road; I am the one who keeps the rule that nobody goes. You are not Oskel. The rule is ours. — Start at the shieling. The herders keep a fire there for the mine, whatever they tell you, and it went out the night she walked.

choices.text: I'll go up to the shieling.
Not now.

q_askes_tune_accept.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
q_askes_tune_accept.text: Knock on the marker stone on your way past. It likes to know who is coming. I have never known what it does when somebody does not.

q_askes_tune_decide_keep_the_fire.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
q_askes_tune_decide_keep_the_fire.text: Always, with a herder beside it and a spare peat stack, and I will knock twice on the marker, so it knows we have understood. It is not an answer. It is a fire. Fires are what Oskel have.

q_askes_tune_decide_teach_her_the_verse.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
q_askes_tune_decide_teach_her_the_verse.text: Our verse over their tune. — Dunna will say a child learns the Rope-Song at eleven. Dunna can come down the pass and say it to my face. Aske will have it by midwinter.

q_askes_tune_decide_send_her_to_the_saye.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
q_askes_tune_decide_send_her_to_the_saye.text: To the Spire, to the Oskel woman who reads lips from the mine years. — She will be frightened of the city and it will be good for her. I will take her myself. I have never been. I will be frightened too.

q_askes_tune_decide.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
q_askes_tune_decide.text: They hum it. — And my child hums it at her porridge. — The fire stops it for a night, and we have kept that fire for a hundred years and called it the herders' and never once said why. — I am the lead-captain. I am hard and fair and I laugh too much for an Oskel. Tell me what a lead-captain does with a tune.

choices.text: Keep the fire lit, always, and a herder by it.
Teach her Oskel's verse, to hum over it.
Send her to Ismay Ondrael.
Let me think on it.

work_going.speaker: Ebba ko-Oskel
work_going.text: A lead-captain keeps a list. Here it is, and I laughed at none of it, which is rare.

greetings.text: The fire burns day and night with a herder beside it, and I knock twice on the marker going past. Aske hums less. When she does, the fire leans towards her.
Aske has Oskel's verse by heart and hums it over the tune until the tune gives up. Dunna came down the pass to say eleven. She heard the child and went back up without saying it.
I took her to the Spire myself. We were both frightened. Ismay Ondrael writes that Aske reads the tune off a slate faster than any Sayer. I do not know if that is good. She sounds happy.
